sources.news_title: US Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to block California ballots
sources.text:
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 — The US Supreme Court on Monday rejected a Trump administration emergency bid to force California to set aside the mail-in ballots of more than 20,000 people on the grounds they may not be American citizens.
Acting a day before the US midterm elections, the top court denied the request in an unsigned, one-sentence ruling, as is common in urgent cases before the court. It gave no reasoning for the decision.
The federal government had accused California of having 190,000 illegal voters on its rolls. It recently revised the figure to 20,000 and filed an emergency lawsuit — after early voting had begun — to stop the state from sending ballots to them.
The Supreme Court action came after lower courts last week — and again on Monday — rejected the demand by the Department of Justice (DOJ), with one judge calling it brazen pre-election interference.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer, in an emergency filing with the Supreme Court, had said that “once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back.”
The California ballot case appeared to be another attempt by the administration to cast doubt on the results of Tuesday’s vote, in which President Donald Trump’s Republican Party is at risk of losing control of Congress.
Trump — who has never acknowledged his own election defeat by Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 — has been claiming for months that there will be fraud in the midterms.
US District Judge David Carter last week refused to order the seizure of the ballots and sided with the government of Democratic-led California.
“The DOJ’s actions are indicative of a broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials,” Carter said.
Another district judge, James Boasberg, also ruled against the Trump administration on Monday, saying the lists of alleged non-citizens were “flawed.”
Sullivan vs Sullivan
A controversy similar to California’s arose in neighbouring Nevada. The administration said initially it had identified 16,000 non-citizen voters there, but after verification procedures that number dropped to 185 — and then to zero.
Studies repeatedly show that while cases of voter fraud exist, such incidents are extremely rare and do not influence election results.
In another closely-watched election case, a federal judge in Alaska over the weekend tossed out a bid by the Trump administration to hold up US Senate election results in the state should the Democratic candidate win.
The DOJ had asked the court to block certification of the results if Republican Dan Sullivan, the incumbent, loses on Tuesday because a second candidate also named Dan Sullivan would have siphoned off votes.
Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Alaska, has denied recruiting the second Sullivan into the race, but The New York Times reported that members of her campaign staff had been involved. — AFP

(The Daily Signal)—Lawsuits on the eve of Election Day are giving courts a brief time window to make influential decisions before final votes are cast.
The Supreme Court on Monday denied a last-minute emergency appeal by the Justice Department to set aside more than 20,000 ballots of suspected noncitizens in California.
Meanwhile, lower court judges are still deciding on other Trump administration election law enforcement efforts and a lawsuit alleging voter confusion in a critical Alaska Senate race.
SCOTUS and 20,000 Noncitizens in California
The Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Justice Department’s request to require that California temporarily set aside mail ballots of more than 20,000 suspected noncitizens until their legal status can be verified.
The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals and the district court rejected the administration in the case, asserting that states have the primary authority over elections.
On Monday, the Justice Department announced the arrest of another six foreign nationals for registering to vote and for voting in Los Angeles County. The criminal matter is not related to the civil case, but First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli of the Central District of California said the department has charged 34 defendants in “Operation Protect the Vote.”
Democrats Demanding State Sovereignty
In another lawsuit, Democrat groups, led by the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, sued the Justice Department for warning state election officials of legal liability if they knowingly counted illegal votes.
Democrats alleged that the Justice Department interfered with state authority over elections. The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia will likely have to decide on the lawsuit before voting closes on Election Day.
The case primarily centered on the Justice Department’s demands that California set aside more than 20,000 ballots of suspected noncitizens and that Washington state set aside more than 400 ballots cast by suspected noncitizens. The Justice Department filed a motion Sunday challenging the standing of Democrat groups.
“Not only do the DOJ letters not create a formal rule, but they have no legal effect on their own as the letters themselves do not tabulate ballots, segregate ballots, or alter any individual’s voter registration status,” the DOJ response said.
Other plaintiffs in the case included the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the Democratic Governors Association, and Democrat leaders in the House and Senate, Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, both of New York.
Challenging Federal Election Monitors
On another front, the NAACP sued the Trump administration Sunday to bar federal agents from serving as election monitors. The Justice Department plans to deploy at least 1,000 election monitors across the United States.
A hearing was held in the case Monday afternoon in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.
The plaintiffs asked the court to prohibit the Justice Department “shall not order any agent, investigator or other employee of a law enforcement agency to” carry a firearm near a polling site, wear a badge, or have a camera.
The Justice Department first began deploying federal election monitors after the 1965 Voting Rights Act. The number of monitors deployed has generally been fewer; in 2016, the Justice Department announced the deployment of about 500 election monitors. However, in 2004, the department deployed 1,996 election monitors.
A department spokesperson told the Daily Signal last week that there were no plans for armed agents near polling sites.
Lawyers for the plaintiffs include Kristen Clarke, the controversial former Biden administration assistant attorney general for the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division.
Appealing ‘Decoy Dan’ Litigation
On Sunday, a federal judge in Alaska dismissed on procedural grounds the Justice Department’s lawsuit regarding the candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan, who is running against Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan, R-Alaska.
The Justice Department appealed the decision to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
Last week, The New York Times first reported that campaign aides to Democrat Senate candidate Mary Peltola were behind recruiting another candidate named Dan Sullivan to run for Senate and draw votes from the incumbent senator under the state’s ranked-choice voting system.
New Mexico Voter Guides
A New Mexico state court was expected to rule before Election Day on a lawsuit the Republican National Committee filed Thursday against the state’s Democrat secretary of state, Maggie Toulouse Oliver, to stop what it called misleading voter guides from being handed out inside polling places.
The RNC alleges that the guides, created by the New Mexico League of Women Voters, show Republican Senate candidate Larry Marker running in a different contest and feature another candidate’s face next to his name. The lawsuit calls for Oliver, the state’s chief election official, to stop distribution.
Marker is challenging Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., in a contest that isn’t seen as competitive. The legal dispute is based on Oliver’s decision to reverse a previous New Mexico policy that kept voter guides created by private organizations away from polling places.
“New Mexico voters are being handed a guide at the polls that puts another candidate’s face next to Republican Senate candidate Larry Marker’s name. That is unacceptable,” RNC Chairman Joe Gruters said in a statement about the lawsuit. “We’re taking Maggie Toulouse Oliver to court to stop it and make sure New Mexico voters can cast their ballots without being fed false information at the polls.”
Neither the New Mexico secretary of state’s office nor the New Mexico League of Women Voters responded to inquiries from the Daily Signal on Monday.

sources.news_title: SUPREME COURT SHUTS DOWN Trump Ballot Segregation Bid One Day Before Midterms
sources.text:
The Supreme Court on Monday rejected an emergency request from the Trump administration to force California to segregate more than 20,000 mail-in ballots flagged for potential noncitizen voting, just one day before the midterm elections.
Justice Elena Kagan denied the application without comment and referred it to the full Court, which rejected it with no noted dissents, according to Democracy Docket. The decision came hours after the Department of Justice filed its appeal, leaving California's vote-counting procedures in place as polls open Tuesday.
The DOJ had asked the high court to intervene after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the request Friday, with Judge Patrick Bumatay dissenting, and a federal judge in Los Angeles issued a similar ruling last week. The administration argued that segregating the ballots would preserve them for review without canceling any votes.
"Once illegally cast ballots are counted and commingled with lawful votes, the resulting harm is impossible to remedy," the Department of Justice wrote in its filing.
California officials say their safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and contend the federal list may contain errors that could disenfranchise eligible voters. Data scientists working with an immigrants rights group told Democracy Docket on Saturday that the government's list was missing the state voter identification number — described as the "single most critical column" — and included mismatched dates, dozens of U.S. citizens, and thousands of people not currently registered to vote in California.
The case stems from an Oct. 15 DOJ lawsuit alleging California is impeding enforcement of a federal law barring noncitizens from voting in federal elections. The administration claims the state violated the Constitution's Supremacy Clause. On Monday evening, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., said it was "likely" the Trump administration violated the Constitution by taking over election responsibilities from the states and Congress, according to Fox News Politics.
Next News Network flagged the developing fight earlier Monday on X, noting that the DOJ was weighing a Supreme Court filing before Election Day. "California counts for weeks, so DOJ is the only one in a hurry," the post read. A second post confirmed the administration had asked the justices to stop California from counting the flagged ballots — a request the Court declined to grant.
The dispute unfolds amid a broader administration push to influence how states run elections, including demands for access to voter rolls and warnings that officials could face prosecution for knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote. California, the nation's most populous state, holds 52 House seats. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of the chamber.
The Supreme Court's rejection marks the third time this fall it has declined to intervene in Trump-backed election measures, following decisions in September that blocked restrictions on mail voting and threw out Missouri's congressional gerrymander, according to Democracy Docket. More than 6 million early votes have already been cast in California.
Our Take
Patriots, read that ruling carefully. The Supreme Court just told the federal government it cannot set aside 20,000 ballots flagged as potentially cast by noncitizens — and it did so on the eve of an election, without a single justice noting a dissent.
That should trouble every American who believes only citizens should decide American elections. The DOJ's argument was modest: hold the ballots aside while eligibility is checked, don't cancel a single vote. The Court said no. Now those ballots get commingled with lawful votes, and as the DOJ warned, the harm becomes impossible to remedy.
California and its allies insist the federal list is riddled with errors and that their safeguards work. Maybe. But the remedy for an error is to check the list — not to count the ballots and sort it out later. The Left has spent years telling us noncitizen voting is a myth while fighting every attempt to verify it. Why the panic over a simple audit?
The Constitution's Supremacy Clause means what it says. Federal law bars noncitizens from voting in federal elections. The executive branch has the authority to enforce that law — or it is supposed to. Instead, three times this fall the high court has sided with the states and the party machinery over the administration's election-integrity efforts.
So here's the question every voter should carry into the voting booth Tuesday: if the federal government cannot even set aside a ballot pending a citizenship check, what exactly is it allowed to do to secure our elections? And who benefits from that answer?

sources.news_title: Supreme Court rejects Trump administration’s bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — Acting quickly and emphatically, the Supreme Court on Monday turned down the Trump administration’s bid to set aside ballots from 20,000 California voters who the administration says may not be citizens.
Without a comment or dissent, the justices dismissed the emergency appeal.
It is a rare rebuke for Trump’s lawyers to have such an appeal turned away.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer had appealed Monday and said the court must “segregate” these California ballots before they are counted.
The appeal went to Justice Elena Kagan, who oversees the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals. In the normal course, she could have asked California’s lawyers to respond.
Instead, the court issued a one-line order. “The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied,” it said.
It is only the latest defeat of defeats.
The administration had lost before a federal judge in Los Angeles and twice at the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco.
Those judges said that President Trump’s lawyers were wrong on the Constitution and that their complaint came too late for this election.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom blasted the administration’s appeal after repeatedly being denied its requested relief in lower courts as baseless, and the government’s claim of an emergency as dubious given their own actions in recent days.
“Trump and his administration have never understood what ‘NO’ means, and it appears after being told ‘NO’ three times last week they’re still unsure. After they sat on this for more than three days, they now ask for ‘emergency’ relief on the eve of the election,” Newsom wrote on X. “Just another reason their claims are bogus.”
In May, more than 23 million Californians were registered to vote, and the majority lean in favor of Democrats. But Trump claimed again last week “there are hundreds of thousands of bad ballots, bad votes, in California. Millions, in my opinion.”
More than 6.4 million ballots had already been cast as of Sunday, according to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber’s office. Those ballots are already being counted, per California law.
In mid-October, the Trump administration sued and said federal courts should require California and Los Angeles County to “set aside vote-by-mail ballots from persons identified by the federal government likely to be non-citizens.”
The lawsuit was filed just days after Justice Department officials gave Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan a 48-hour deadline to begin cooperating with federal authorities to set aside ballots from about 20,000 voters the administration had determined may not be citizens.
Weber, Logan and a host of other voter advocacy groups and elections experts have questioned the reliability of the administration’s list, which was compiled using a mix of voter data purchased from California and taken from commercial platforms, according to administration officials.
County officials and analysts with the UCLA Voting Rights Project have said the lists contain U.S. citizens and others who are not registered to vote.
Los Angeles County officials have said a review of a subset of 200 voter registrations from the 20,000-person list found that nearly 40% appeared to have been born in the United States, and that 71.2% showed no record of ever voting. A UCLA analysis of the 20,000 names found that more than 4 in 10 weren’t on California’s current voter roll.
Attorneys for the state have argued that complying with the administration’s demands while voting is already underway would be impossible without causing widespread disruptions to the election, and would disenfranchise legitimate voters incorrectly swept up into the administration’s unreliable lists.
Justice Department officials have stressed that they are only asking for ballots from the flagged voters to be set aside while state and federal authorities work together to determine whether the voters are citizens — which they have said could be accomplished relatively quickly if the state would simply comply with its requests to collaborate.
They have also said emergency intervention from the courts is necessary because California law allows ballots to be counted before election day, and once a ballot is cast in person or removed from its mail envelope, it cannot be resegregated from the vote total.
Federal law says that within 90 days of an election, officials may not “systematically remove the names of ineligible voters from the official lists of eligible voters.”
Separately, the Supreme Court also has repeatedly frowned on “late-breaking, court-ordered rule changes” involving elections.
The California court cases have put a spotlight on the state versus federal divide in election law.
Usually, federal laws are deemed to be the “supreme law” and override state laws that are in conflict. No one disputes that U.S. prosecutors may bring criminal fraud charges against noncitizens who violate a federal law by registering with a state to vote and casting an illegal ballot.
But election rules and procedures are different. The Constitution says “the Times, Places and Manner of holding elections for Senators and Representatives shall be prescribed in each state,” unless Congress acts by law to “alter” its regulations.
The 9th Circuit judges in Friday’s opinion said that “this clause expressly dictates which sovereign has the authority to prescribe the manner in which congressional elections are conducted.”
“If the United States believes different procedures are necessary for vote-by-mail ballots, we believe it should take that suggestion to Congress, not the courts,” said Judges Mark J. Bennett, a Trump appointee, and Gabriel P. Sanchez, a Biden appointee.
Dissenting Judge Patrick J. Bumatay, a Trump appointee, called the administration’s proposal to separate the 20,000 ballots a “reasonable request” and a “modest remedy” for the problem of illegal voting.
The majority cited a 2013 opinion written by the late Justice Antonin Scalia.
“The Elections Clause functions as a default provision,” he wrote. “It invests the states with responsibility for the mechanics of congressional elections,” unless Congress adopts a different rule.
Scalia spoke for a 7-2 majority that rejected an Arizona law that required voters to show documentary proof of their citizenship when registering to vote. In the National Voter Registration Act of 1993, Congress said voters may register to vote by filling out a form and attesting under oath they are citizens.
California does the same under state law.
Scalia said the federal voter registration law did not allow Arizona to adopt new and stricter rules.
In dissent, conservative Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel A. Alito Jr. said they would go further to protect the states from federal interference in elections.
“Given states’ exclusive authority to set voter qualifications and to determine whether those qualifications are met,” Thomas said, the Arizona restriction should have been upheld.
“The Constitution reserves for the States the power to decide who is qualified to vote in federal elections,” Alito added.
Last month, Trump’s prosecutors brought fraud charges against 28 lawful immigrants in California who are alleged to have registered or voted in the past even though they are not citizens. They did so under a 1996 immigration law that makes it “unlawful for any alien” to vote in a federal election.
Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, in a post Monday on X, wrote that California “has refused to work with the federal government to protect against non-citizen voting, which dilutes lawful votes.
“We will continue pursuing every available legal avenue to protect the integrity of our elections and ensure federal law is enforced,” he wrote.
Election law experts were quick to slam the Justice Department’s intervention.
“The Supreme Court should and I believe will reject the administration’s nervy last-minute attempts to meddle in California’s elections,” said Walter Olson at the libertarian Cato Institute. “Mar-a-Lago, which has been calling the shots on this, needs to get this through its head: unless and until Congress provides clear legal guidance to the contrary, the Constitution reserves these decisions to the states.”
The notion of segregating potentially suspect ballots is not a new issue for the Supreme Court.
In November 2020, Alito agreed with Pennsylvania state officials and said they should set aside late-arriving mail ballots to be counted separately.
In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, state election officials and the state Supreme Court agreed to waive part of the state’s law and allow for counting mail ballots that arrived up to three days late.
Republicans strongly objected. That led to Alito’s order. But in the end, the small number of late votes made no difference because the Democratic candidate, former Vice President Joe Biden, decisively won Pennsylvania’s votes and defeated Trump.
The California dispute is different because the state has not changed its voting rules or election procedures. Instead, it is the Trump administration that sought a late change in California’s voting rules and election procedures.

Supreme Court Rejects Trump Emergency Intervention in California Elections
sources.text:
Only a few hours after the Trump administration sought an emergency order this Monday to require California election officials to set aside the ballots of 20,000 alleged noncitizens pending verification of their citizenship, the Supreme Court issued an unsigned ruling rejecting the case out of hand. No explanation was included, no hearing held. In fact, the court never even sought a response from any of involved state agencies that had resisted such demands.
Given that the emergency application was submitted just a day before Election Day, the ruling should not come as a great surprise. Federal voting law seriously frowns on any changes made in election protocol within 90 days of the election day. In addition, the U.S. Constitution explicitly empowers states to establish the time, place, and manner in which elections will be held. To the extent it countenances any federal intervention, the Constitution assigns that authority only to Congress and not to the Executive branch.
Attorneys for the White House argued that federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections. By setting aside the ballots the Department of Homeland Security determined were “likely” cast by noncitizens, federal attorneys insisted no votes would be canceled. They termed the last-minute intervention a “modest solution.”
The emergency petition was submitted to the Supreme Court just one day before Tuesday’s midterm elections in which the Republican Party and the White House are in risk of losing both the House and Senate majorities. But just last week, the Department of Justice was rebuffed no fewer than three times while making the same argument; two of those times were by a three-judge panel of the U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals and one by lower court judge David O. Carter. In all three instances, the judges found that the U.S. Constitution gave sole authority over the time place and manner by which elections are held to the state in which the elections are held. To the extent there’s any variance allowed, they ruled, the constitution spells out that only Congress — not the President — is empowered to impose such changes.
Attorneys for the Department of Justice argued that the ballots submitted by “likely” noncitizens needed to be set aside or else the votes of actual citizens will be diluted by illegally cast ballots. Judge Carter and the panel of appellate judges expressed doubt about the basis by which the DOJ asserted the 20,000 ballots were of “unlikely” origin.
Over the weekend, the UCLA Voting Rights Project announced that data analysis of the voting list revealed that more than 42 percent of the names on the list are not listed anywhere on the state’s active voter rolls. Local and state election officials have argued the list contains an undisclosed number of names of U.S.-born citizens.
Of the 20,000 alleged non-citizens casting ballots, 180 reportedly originated in Santa Barbara County. To date Santa Barbara County’s elections chief Joe Holland — independently elected — has declined to make any public statement on the matter nor has anyone else in his office. No other Santa Barbara County official has either.
They did, however, release the original DOJ letter demanding that the county verify the citizenship of the 180 individuals and that they do so within 48 hours of receipt. Any election official that declined to cooperate, the letter threatened, would be guilty of violating federal election law and would be held as legally responsible as anyone who voted illegally.
Judge Carter strongly cautioned the DOJ against threatening county or state elections officials attempting to do their jobs. To impose last-minute changes to the way counties count their ballots, he ruled, threatened to put the state’s entire vote counting infrastructure into chaos. This chaos, coupled with the threat of an investigation, Carter cautioned, could have a chilling effect on people exercising their right to vote, itself a violation of federal voting law. In addition, he noted, federal voting law prohibits any change in voting procedure enacted within 90 days of the election in question.
Instead, Carter said, he would appoint a special master to help him sort out how many of the ballots, if any, were cast by noncitizens. This could take place after the election was over, he pointed out, because counties have until December 13 to certify their changes election results.
In San Lous Obispo County, the elections chief had announced last week she had no intention of complying with the DOJ’s command and investigating the citizenship of 63 alleged noncitizens. The District Attorney of S.L.O., however, volunteered to investigate the citizenship of those named by the DOJ. In response, Santa Barbara DA John Savrnoch stated he had no intention of doing anything of the kind. Nor had he been asked to do so.

In summary
The U.S. Supreme Court declined to issue an emergency ruling in the Trump Administration’s case to sequester 20,000 ballots. Here’s what to know about the ongoing, unprecedented legal attack on California’s elections.
On the eve of Election Day, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear a last-minute legal challenge from the Trump administration that would have forced California to not count over 20,000 ballots that the administration had flagged as being cast by possible noncitizens.
The rejection came the same day prosecutors filed new federal charges against noncitizens accused of voting improprieties.
Here’s where things stand on the unprecedented legal war the federal government is waging on California’s elections.
U.S. Supreme Court rejects Trump
On Monday — a day before the election — the Trump Administration appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, which almost immediately rejected the federal government’s request to force California to set aside the 20,000 ballots.
None of the judges dissented, and no explanation was provided.
The ruling came after U.S. District Court Judge David O. Carter issued a blistering ruling last week declaring that the Trump administration’s efforts were likely unconstitutional.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” wrote Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton.
The Trump administration immediately appealed to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals. A three-judge panel on the appellate court for the second time in a week rejected the administration’s claims.
Background on the case
For years, President Donald Trump has claimed, without evidence, that potentially “millions” of noncitizen voters are rigging elections for Democrats. His federal prosecutors in California have been aggressively trying to prove him right, even as independent experts and election officials say noncitizen voting is exceedingly rare.
In mid-October, the Trump administration sent a letter to California’s secretary of state and Los Angeles County election officials demanding they set aside the 20,000 ballots. The letter demanded the ballots not be counted until the voters’ citizenship can be verified.
California refused.
The Trump administration sued and urged a federal court to issue an order forcing California to comply. Meanwhile, it also sent similar demand letters and grand jury subpoenas to county elections offices warning that election workers could be charged if they allow noncitizens to vote.

New arrests on eve of Election Day
Also on Monday, the federal government announced charges against another 12 noncitizens for registering to vote or voting in California elections after previously charging 28 green California card holders for similar crimes.
“Voting is the essence of American citizenship,” Bill Essayli, Trump’s top prosecutor in Los Angeles, said at a press conference Monday. “Illegally attempting to infiltrate and influence our political determinations is not only wrong, it’s a crime.”
California officials have been quick to point out that the arrests represent a fraction of a percent of California’s 23 million registered voters — hardly proof of a sweeping election-rigging conspiracy as Trump has so often claimed.
“They said, ‘Aha! Look at this widespread voter fraud,’ and then they made 28 arrests,” Democratic California Attorney General Rob Bonta said last week. “I mean, talk about a fizzle.”
Moria Dahan, one of the people charged on Monday, made her first appearance in federal court shortly after the charges were announced. Dahan was shackled at the ankles and led into the courtroom by U.S. marshals. Dahan, an Israeli national who lives in West Hills, spoke through a Hebrew interpreter as she acknowledged the charges against her. She was released minutes later.
Her attorney, Tiffany Feder, said her client didn’t “intend to defraud, intend to conceal, or falsify any kind of documents. She didn’t know what she was filling out.”
Judge blocks election worker threats
Another federal court judge issued an order Friday blocking the Trump administration’s unprecedented targeting of election workers, after their union filed a legal challenge asking the court to halt the administration’s threats.
U.S. District Court Judge Trina L. sources.text:
Supreme Court rejects Trump's push to invalidate more than 20,000 California ballots
US Supreme Court rejects Trump, lets California count all ballots.
Nov 2 (Reuters) - Acting on the eve of the US midterm elections, the Supreme Court quickly rejected on Monday a bid by President Donald Trump's administration to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters who federal officials allege are likely non-US citizens.
The justices denied the Justice Department's emergency request just hours after it filed it, shutting down the administration's claims over disputed ballots that could have affected thousands of voters and injected uncertainty into election outcomes.
The decision represented another defeat for Trump as his fellow Republicans fight to retain control of Congress in Tuesday's midterms. California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold.
The administration intensified its focus on alleged noncitizen voting in the run-up to the midterms. Multiple studies and state audits show that ineligible voting, including by noncitizens, is rare.
The Supreme Court's brief, one-sentence order on Monday did not offer any explanation of its action, as is common when it handles emergency matters. No justice publicly dissented from the decision. The court also did not ask California for a response to the administration's request, a step that, when taken, usually signals serious consideration of an emergency case.
A federal appeals court refused the administration's request on Friday.
"Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," the Justice Department said in its request to the Supreme Court.
The administration had demanded that California separate any allegedly unlawful ballots from other ballots and not count them until those voters are determined to be US citizens.
"This latest move reeks of desperation, and is another attempt to undermine our elections and trample on the rule of law," California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said in a statement after the administration's filing earlier in the day, vowing to "defend the fundamental right to vote and push back against this lawlessness."
Trump has made false claims about widespread US voting fraud including in the 2020 election lost to Democrat Joe Biden.
"We will continue pursuing every available legal avenue to protect the integrity of our elections and ensure federal law is enforced," acting US Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a social media post after the administration's filing earlier in the day.
CONSTITUTIONAL QUESTIONS
The US Constitution assigns the responsibility of administering elections to states, though the federal government has some oversight. The lawsuit marked a rare federal intervention in the voting process and signaled a willingness by the administration to contest the election results in court.
The administration already sought to restrict voting by mail — a mode of casting ballots used more often by Democratic-leaning voters — but the Supreme Court in September rebuffed that effort. And a federal judge on Sunday dismissed the administration's lawsuit concerning the US Senate race in Alaska.
The list of 20,000 registered voters was amassed by the US Department of Homeland Security and sent to California officials and to Los Angeles County officials.
The Justice Department sued in federal court on October 15, claiming California is unlawfully preventing its enforcement of a 1996 US law that makes it a criminal offense for noncitizens to vote in federal elections. The department said California's action violated the Constitution's Supremacy Clause, which holds that federal law generally preempts state law.
California has said that the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and that the lawsuit threatens to deprive 20,000 people of their right to vote based on vague accusations. The administration's process for scrutinizing voter lists to identify noncitizens is flawed and likely rife with errors, it said in court papers.
California has 52 seats in the House of Representatives, more than any other state. Democrats need a net gain of four House seats to win a majority in the chamber.
'BEND TO THE WILL'
US District Judge David Carter in Los Angeles denied the administration's request on October 28.
"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch," Carter wrote.
Carter raised concerns over the reliability of the administration's data, noting that people recently flagged by the federal government as noncitizens on voter rolls in other states have repeatedly turned out to be naturalized US citizens.
"If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," Carter wrote.
The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals also refused on Friday to block the ballots, emphasizing the state's power over election procedures and California's "comprehensive statutory scheme to ensure the integrity of its elections," including a system for canceling registrations if a voter is shown to be ineligible.
The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach toward how states run elections. The Justice Department has told election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allow noncitizens to remain on their rolls or cast ballots. But it also has lost a series of lawsuits seeking to obtain voter rolls, including sensitive personal information, from dozens of states.
(Reporting by Andrew Chung; Editing by Will Dunham)

(The Center Square) - The U.S. Supreme Court rejected an appeal on Monday by the Trump administration to segregate 20,000 California ballots for fears of noncitizen voting in the midterm elections, one day before polls close. 
Lawyers for the U.S. Department of Justice on Monday asked justices to temporarily block an order preventing officials from segregating mail-in ballots ahead of the election. Justice Elena Kagan denied the motion in a brief unsigned order that did not indicate opinions of others on the court. 
Solicitor General John Sauer said segregating the ballots is a necessary step to ensure the integrity of federal elections in California. The state sends mail-in ballots to every registered voter leading up to an election. 
"Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," Sauer wrote in a filing. "The only way to preserve the district court's ability to grant relief to the United States after a full merits proceeding, therefore, is to segregate the challenged ballots now."
Walter Olson, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute, said the Justice Department did not have authority to require California operate under separate guidance based on suspected criminal behavior.
"It is simply physically impossible for the registrars to obey their own California laws and do what the federal government has requested," Olson told The Center Square. 
On Oct. 13, the Justice Department warned the California Secretary of State's Office about 20,000 "highly likely" noncitizen voters. Election officials in California said the effort would create confusion for voters and sow distrust in the system. 
Kiersten Pels, a spokesperson for the Justice Department, told the Center Square 28 people on that list were charged with federal crimes, including lying about their citizenship to vote. 
“What undermines confidence is noncitizens voting,” said Pels. “Eligible citizens are not affected. We asked counties to set aside these ballots, not cancel them, until citizenship is confirmed."
Regardless, Olson said California has a process to ensure noncitizens are not participating in elections. He said the process is administered on an individual basis, rather than purging from a list. Olson doubted the quality of evidence federal officials had on noncitizens voting. 
"They're probably not going to qualify under California's requirement that evidence of extraordinary quality needs to be brought in if you're going to actually stop someone during the voting process," Olson told The Center Square.

sources.news_title: US Supreme Court rejects Trump DOJ’s attempt to freeze California vote counting
sources.text:
US Supreme Court rejects Trump DOJ’s attempt to freeze California vote counting
The U.S. Supreme Court on April 9, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday, mere hours before Election Day in the midterms that will determine control of Congress, denied the Trump administration’s final attempt to force California to set aside the ballots of 20,000 people it suspects are noncitizens.
The decision marked a significant blow to President Donald Trump’s bid to control voting in the country’s most populous state and capped a whirlwind three weeks of legal war between the U.S. Department of Justice and California’s state and local election officials.
The Supreme Court’s denial also removed the possibility of a last-minute ruling that could have led to chaos if officials were forced to scramble to follow the Justice Department’s demands.
The court denied the Justice Department’s request late Monday afternoon in a one-sentence order. It noted no dissents, and offered no reasoning, as is often the case in decisions on emergency requests.
The Justice Department had demanded that election officials set aside the ballots of about 20,000 people on a list developed by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. The DOJ told election officials the ballots shouldn’t be tabulated unless the citizenship of the individuals could be verified.
At the same time, Justice Department lawyers threatened election officials with prosecution if they counted the ballots. The Trump administration argued that the officials would be aiding and abetting noncitizen voting, a misdemeanor federal crime. Election officials in Los Angeles County received grand jury subpoenas.
“Today’s decision is another blow to the Trump administration’s manufactured election emergency and a major victory for local election officials and voters across the country,” Jonathan Miller, chief program officer of Public Rights Project, which represented Los Angeles County, said in a statement.
States and federal government
The dispute pitted the Trump administration’s claims of executive authority against California’s power to run its own elections.
The U.S. Constitution assigns states the responsibility of administering elections, though Congress can override state rules. The president — and by extension the officials under him — have no unilateral power over how states run their elections.
The Justice Department on Monday morning asked for an administrative stay that would have required California to begin segregating ballots of voters on the list while the Trump administration prepares a full appeal. The Supreme Court denied the DOJ’s request without seeking briefing from California and the other parties in the case.
Steve Vladeck, a professor at Georgetown University Law Center and a leading expert on the Supreme Court, wrote on social media that he couldn’t remember any case in which the court denied a Justice Department application without calling for a response.
“That’s an even bigger ‘go away’ than the lack of (public) dissents,” Vladeck wrote.
The DOJ didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the decision.
Avoids major fallout
Election officials warned of grave consequences if they were ordered to separate the ballots. Aman Bhullar, an assistant Los Angeles County registrar-recorder/county clerk, wrote in a court declaration in October that the potential fallout included halting ballot counting and in-person voting.
The Supreme Court generally shies away from ordering major last-minute changes to elections. While the justices have shown greater deference to states that alter their elections, they often counsel federal courts against significant 11th-hour interventions — a doctrine that’s become known as the Purcell principle.
But the Trump administration had argued that because noncitizen voting is illegal under federal law, any ballot cast by a noncitizen is unlawful.
“It also follows that a State may not count such an invalid ballot,” U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in his request.
Stephen Richer, a legal fellow with the Cato Institute’s Robert A. Levy Center for Constitutional Studies, noted in a statement that every California voter attests to their citizenship under penalty of perjury — the same requirement in federal law.
“The federal government has suspicions — not proof — that certain voters are not citizens,” Richer wrote. “California law provides a process for challenging those voters. The federal government cannot invent its own at this late hour.”
List questioned
The accuracy of the list also came under intense criticism from California election officials and voting rights advocates.
An immigrant rights group, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, said in a court filing Saturday that an analysis by data experts found that 42% of the names weren’t found on California’s current voter file. At least 22 names on the DHS list match names of U.S. citizens compiled by the organization, the analysis found.
The Justice Department said Homeland Security used a public copy of California’s voter roll to develop the list. DHS checked the list against federal records and used the Lexis Nexis research service to analyze voter information, the Trump administration said in court filings.
The DOJ repeatedly argued that once a ballot is processed, it becomes impossible to identify whether a noncitizen cast it. Yet the department didn’t ask the Supreme Court to intervene until Monday morning, days after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against the set-aside request on Friday.
When Sauer did file a request with the Supreme Court, he wrote that his office had been “informed” that the Trump administration identified more than 20,000 individuals “who appear to be registered as voters in California at the time the voter-roll information was received and whom the United States believes are likely to be aliens.”
Sauer’s arguments were undercut by remarks made by a Justice Department lawyer hours later.
During a court hearing in California on Monday over the Trump administration’s threats against election officials, Kenneth Kao, an assistant U.S. attorney, acknowledged the list contains significant errors.
“Would you agree there’s a high error rate — not nominal — but a high error rate,” Judge Trina Thompson, an appointee of President Joe Biden in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, asked.
“I think that’s a fair statement,” Kao replied.

The Supreme Court on Monday quickly denied the Trump administration’s request to segregate the ballots of 20,000 California voters the federal government suspects are “potential noncitizen voters.”
The one-line order was issued without the justices asking for a response from California officials and without any justices noting a dissent to the denial.
The DOJ application came the day before Election Day and urged the high court to intervene to keep the suspected ballots separate from lawful ones. An election law expert predicted that the Supreme Court would not want to get involved in any last-ditch efforts regarding the midterms.
“They don’t want any part of this nonsense,” Justin Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Law School, told The Washington Sun. “If there were an actual case that involved actual disruptions or actual claims on actual law, maybe, but none of these do.”

The high court did not detail its reasoning, as is common in emergency decisions. The justices previously rejected Trump’s push to restrict mail ballots around the country in September, even though the justices have sided with his administration in a series of other emergency docket appeals.
The Republican Trump administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite them being rare.

“The Executive Branch has likely violated the Constitution’s Elections Clause, which commits authority over election rules to the states and Congress alone,” wrote Chief Judge James Boasberg.
The administration, for its part, said segregating the ballots was a modest request that would eventually allow legal votes to still be counted.

The Justice Department has sought to move the case along quickly, unsuccessfully asking an appeals court to intervene early.

The administration claims that these individuals are “likely” noncitizens, but that they are nonetheless registered to vote in California.

Shortly after receiving Trump’s list, Los Angeles County officials took a sample of 200 names from the list to see if they are actually noncitizens who appear on the state’s voter rolls. In their preliminary review, they determined that nearly 40 percent of the names on the list belong to people who were born in the United States (and thus are almost certainly US citizens), and that 56 percent of the individuals on the list either canceled their registration or their registration is no longer active. But it is still unclear what Trump is trying to accomplish by bringing the California case to the justices on the day before an election, when even this Supreme Court is unlikely to rule in Trump’s favor.
If this is the extent of Trump’s efforts to overturn an election that is expected to end badly for his Republican Party, then those efforts are unlikely to amount to anything at all.

Trump’s DOJ asks US Supreme Court to rule in California voting case
The U.S. Department of Justice logo is displayed on a speaker’s podium. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)
The U.S. Department of Justice on Monday asked the U.S. Supreme Court to require California to set aside the ballots of suspected noncitizen voters in a last-ditch appeal by the Trump administration to exert control over the state’s vote counting.
The request came on the eve of Election Day and as more than 5 million mail ballots have already been cast in California, a state where voters are expected to elect dozens of Democrats to the U.S. House.
California’s election could be thrown into chaos if the Supreme Court grants the request. State and local election officials have previously warned that they have no easy way to quickly identify and set aside the ballots of individuals on the list.
In the Trump administration’s emergency application, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer noted that federal law prohibits voting by noncitizens, who still do sometimes vote “despite that prohibition,” he wrote.
“Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back,” Sauer added.
Logistically difficult
As a universal vote-by-mail state, every voter in California is sent a mail ballot. While millions of these ballots have already been returned, millions more may be dropped off on Tuesday or arrive by mail in the coming days.
Aman Bhullar, an assistant Los Angeles County registrar-recorder/county clerk, warned in a court declaration in October that the Trump administration’s request could wreak havoc on elections.
“The potential consequences of implementing DOJ’s demand are severe and range from halting all counting; halting in-person voters’ ability to cast votes; or otherwise interfering with the ability to accurately count votes,” Bhullar wrote.
Already a week ago, Shelby Wayment, staff attorney at the University of California, Los Angeles Safeguarding Democracy Project, questioned the feasibility of the DOJ’s demands. Ballots have already been mailed out and were being processed, she said.
“Just logistically, I don’t think it’s possible at this point,” Wayment said in a late October interview.
No widespread fraud
The Justice Department sued California in October, alleging that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security had identified 20,000 suspected noncitizen voters. California officials raised concerns about the veracity of the list, and declined to take action based on it.
An immigrant rights group, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, has raised serious concerns about the list after a judge forced the Trump administration to share a copy with the organization.
The group said in a court filing Saturday that an analysis by data experts found that 42% of the names weren’t found on California’s current voter file. At least 22 names on the list match names of U.S. citizens compiled by the organization, the analysis found.
“There is no widespread voter fraud. The federal government has no right to interfere in California’s elections,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said in a statement on Saturday.
11th hour challenge
The Justice Department has said the Department of Homeland Security compiled the list by checking a public copy of California’s voter file against federal records and information from the research service Lexis Nexis.
A district court judge and the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals have both ruled against the Trump administration in the case. State and local officials have argued the Justice Department exceeded its authority because states administer elections under the U.S. Constitution.
Even though the 9th Circuit issued a decision on Friday, the Justice Department didn’t ask the Supreme Court to intervene until midday Monday, less than 24 hours before Election Day.
The Justice Department has asked for an administrative stay that would require California to begin segregating ballots of voters on the list while the Trump administration prepares a full appeal. While it’s unknown how the Supreme Court will rule, in general the justices frown on federal courts ordering major last-minute changes to elections.
Because the case arises out of the 9th Circuit, Justice Elena Kagan, one of the court’s three liberals, will be the first to review the application.
Walter Olsen, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute’s Robert A. Levy Center for Constitutional Studies, in a statement predicted the Supreme Court will reject the request. He argued that the Justice Department is asking California officials to violate their own state laws.
“The Supreme Court should and I believe will reject the administration’s nervy last-minute attempts to meddle in California’s elections, as lower courts have rejected them,” Olsen said.

President Donald Trump’s top Supreme Court lawyer distanced himself from Attorney General Todd Blanche’s claims about 20,000 likely noncitizen voters in California.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote three times that his office had been “informed” of the list’s findings, according to his emergency application to the justices.

But Sauer’s filing credits those findings to others, treating Blanche's Justice Department as his client.
“In this case, this Office has been informed that the United States has identified more than 20,000 individuals who appear to be registered to vote in California,” Sauer wrote, describing them as likely noncitizens “in the United States’ view.”
Sauer’s filing says three times that his office was 'informed' of what the list found. A Raw Story review of 12 other emergency applications from his office found that wording in only one, used once before in Sept. 2026, about logistical problems with removals.
Blanche, Sauer’s boss at the Justice Department, has called the idea that the department is independent from the White House a “misperception.” “I work for President Trump,” Blanche said on New York Post columnist Miranda Devine’s podcast on Oct. 21, Mediaite reported. Sauer’s careful wording comes one level below an attorney general who says he works for the president.
One critic accused the department of a crime minutes after it announced the filing.
“This crime ... is precisely the crime Trump attempted in 2020,” national security journalist Marcy Wheeler wrote on X, responding to an Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter post announcing the filing. “Only this time, he has corrupt criminals at DOJ willing to do the crime with him.” McCotter’s post said the department would keep “pursuing every available legal avenue to protect the integrity of our elections and ensure federal law is enforced.”
The lawyer now relaying the list defended Trump in his own 2020 election case. As Trump’s personal lawyer, Sauer won him “substantial immunity from criminal prosecution” at the Supreme Court in 2024, after Trump was accused of election fraud and conspiracy over his protest of the 2020 results, CNN reported in May.
In that piece, CNN chief Supreme Court analyst Joan Biskupic described Sauer’s delivery before the justices as “quickfire, confrontational and imbued with MAGA attitude.”
A federal judge has already ordered the department to stop threatening California election officials with prosecution. U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson found on Oct. 30 that the plaintiffs were likely to show violations of federal voter-intimidation protections, the Davis Vanguard reported. The department has appealed, according to Just Security’s litigation tracker.
Sauer is asking the justices to order the ballots set aside without deciding whether the people on the list are citizens. After relaying what his office was “informed,” the filing tells the court it “need not resolve any factual disputes about whether any particular individual is a California voter and is an alien or a citizen.”
“If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” U.S. District Judge David O. Carter wrote in denying the request, according to the AP.
“This is a desperate attempt to tilt the electoral playing field,” Amanda Carpenter, a writer and editor at the nonprofit Protect Democracy, wrote on X on Monday.
“This is fascism,” journalist Nancy Levine Stearns wrote on X, sharing a report of the filing.
The filing notes that California keeps accepting mail ballots through Nov. 10. Carter has set a hearing with witnesses on the government’s bid for a preliminary injunction for Nov. 13, three days after that deadline, according to the tracker.

Seeking an extremely fast shadow-docket decision from the Supreme Court, the Trump administration is asked the justices to grant them emergency relief in their quest to sequester 20,000 California mail-in ballots that they say came from suspected non-citizens.
The political theater continued Monday over 20,000 ballots that are not even likely to be consequential in any major races in a state of 23 million registered voters. And lower courts, including the Ninth Circuit court of appeals, have already repeatedly denied the Trump Administration's last-ditch effort to cast doubt on California's elections, and to potentially disenfranchise citizens trying to cast legitimate ballots.
As CBS News reports, the administration appealed to the Supreme Court on Monday, one day ahead of Election Day, seeking an emergency ruling that would require postal workers to set aside mail-in ballots from a list of 20,000 suspected non-citizens — a list whose accuracy has been called into question for multiple reasons.
It's unclear how this process would even work, and the effort appears to be just one more effort by President Trump to foment confusion and prepare to call the entire election rigged or unfair when he is unhappy with the results.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer, in today's filing at the Supreme Court, wrote, "Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back." And he said the administration was seeking a "modest remedy" to keep these potentially invalid votes from "diluting" valid ones.
And on Monday afternoon, as CalMatters reports, the Supreme Court declined to hear the government's request in an unsigned order, and no dissents were recorded.
The emergency filing came one week after the Justice Department sent letters to California county registrars and other officials demanding that ballots from these 20,000 purported noncitizens be sequestered. And those letters came a little over a week after the DOJ's unprecedented civil lawsuit demanding that California not tabulate votes from these suspected noncitizens — without explaining how the government had even compiled their list.
"Federal law explicitly prohibits systematic purges of voters in the period before the election. This is because of the great risk of serious mistakes being made and eligible voters being wrongfully removed," wrote UCLA election law professor Rick Hasen in response to the DOJ's efforts.
And legal experts said that the lawsuit itself was fairly inept, in that it did not even cite a federal statute that gives the government grounds for bringing the suit — citing only a law that is meant to criminalize the act of voting by a noncitizen when they commit that act themselves.
"This is a civil lawsuit against a state asking the court to issue injunctive relief requiring the state to take certain actions in order to, I guess, avoid creating the possibility that some individual might commit this crime?" said Sean Morales-Doyle, senior director of the Brennan Center’s Voting Rights and Elections Program, speaking to the Chronicle. He referred to the suit as "another step in an increasingly desperate campaign that is destined to fail."
U.S. District Judge David Carter shot down the DOJ's legal effort last week writing, "Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch. In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too."
Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton, added that the government's list of names did not seem "credible," and he wrote, "Constitutional rights and our democracy are at stake. The public interest favors their protection."

Supreme Court Rejects Trump Bid to Set Aside 20,000 California Ballots
The Supreme Court on Monday turned away the Trump administration’s last-ditch request to make California set aside mail ballots from about 20,000 people the Justice Department flagged as likely noncitizens.
The justices denied the emergency application in a one-line, unsigned order with no noted dissents, CBS News reported. As is common on the court’s emergency docket, the order gave no reasoning.
The court moved so quickly that it did not ask California for its views before ruling, a step it normally takes, according to NBC News. The administration had filed its request only hours earlier.
Without a court order, the flagged ballots will be counted along with the rest. NBC noted that California strips identifying details from a mail ballot once its signature is verified, so those votes could not be traced later.
The Justice Department argued that segregating the ballots would preserve them while their eligibility was investigated, without canceling any votes, Fox News reported. It had gone to the high court after the 9th Circuit refused relief Friday.
“Once illegally cast ballots are counted and commingled with lawful votes, the resulting harm is impossible to remedy,” the department wrote. Judge Patrick Bumatay, a Trump appointee, dissented from the appeals court’s refusal.
Judges Questioned the Government’s List
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, a Clinton appointee, had warned that segregating the ballots would “wreak havoc” on the midterms and erode trust in the democratic process, the Associated Press reported.
“If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” Carter wrote in denying the department’s request last week.
In a separate hearing, U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson asked Justice Department lawyer Kenneth Kao whether the list had “a high error rate.” Kao replied, “That’s a fair statement,” adding that registrars’ help was needed to verify the voters.
Bill Essayli, who runs the department’s Los Angeles office, has defended the list. “This isn’t speculation. This isn’t a theory,” he told reporters, though he later conceded it may contain errors.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said the appeal “reeks of desperation and is another attempt to undermine our elections and trample on the rule of law.”
Also on Monday, Chief U.S. District Judge James Boasberg in Washington blocked further administration demands on California’s mail ballots, writing that the executive branch “has likely violated the Constitution’s Elections Clause.”
The ballot dispute has run for weeks, including two 9th Circuit losses for the department. All of California’s roughly 23 million registered voters are mailed a ballot, and CBS reported that more than 6 million had been returned.
Federal law bars noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Justice Department has charged more than 200 people with voting illegally in past elections. Confirmed cases of noncitizen voting remain rare.

sources.news_title: Trump Justice Dept breaks with tradition to intervene in midterms
sources.text:
Trump Justice Dept breaks with tradition to intervene in midterms
- By Reuters -
- Nov 03, 2026
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump’s Justice Department has shown a willingness to intervene directly in Tuesday’s midterm elections, breaking with decades of practice meant to avoid the appearance that its law enforcement powers are being used to benefit a political party or candidate.
In California, the Justice Department sought to set aside mail-in ballots from about 20,000 voters it alleges are likely non-US citizens ineligible to vote.
The department has also demanded records in a related criminal probe. California has said it has implemented measures to prevent voting by noncitizens and argued the Justice Department does not have the authority to block votes.
In Alaska, the department has intensified a criminal investigation into whether a Senate candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan entered the race to confuse voters. It also sought to block certification if Sullivan narrowly loses, but a federal judge dismissed that lawsuit on Sunday.
Courts have now rejected the department’s lawsuits against both states, but the cases underscore the DOJ’s willingness to intervene in election disputes before votes are counted and results certified. The department has appealed the Alaska decision.
Critics say the department could accelerate any attempt by Trump to sow doubt about the midterms, which will determine control of Congress and the winners of dozens of governors’ races.
“It appears that the administration wants the department to have an impact that was previously prohibited,” said Mark Blumberg, who previously led the DOJ’s election response to civil rights threats and has since founded the Rule of Law Project.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche says the department’s efforts are lawful and aim to protect the integrity of the vote.
“The Department isn’t helping any campaign. It’s enforcing the law,” department spokesperson Kiersten Pels said in a statement.
FALSE FRAUD CLAIMS
The US Constitution assigns responsibility for administering elections to the states, but Trump, a Republican, argues Democratic-led states are not doing enough to prevent voting by noncitizens, which is prohibited under US law. He continues to falsely assert that widespread fraud caused his 2020 election loss. Independent studies and state audits have found voter fraud to be rare.
Outside groups aligned with Trump filed more than 60 lawsuits challenging his 2020 defeat, all of which were unsuccessful. DOJ officials in his first term rejected pressure to enlist the department in those efforts.
“The right-wing fringe outside groups are not going to have to do that this year because the DOJ is clearly standing ready and willing to do it,” said Lis Frost, a voting rights lawyer with Elias Law Group, which frequently represents Democrats in court.
Historically, Justice Department election interventions have focused on enforcing federal laws meant to ensure racial minorities or vulnerable populations can vote without impediment.
THE ALASKA CASE
Alaska has become a particularly intense legal battleground after the New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan to challenge incumbent Dan Sullivan.
The Justice Department lawsuit, which Trump said he directed the department to file, asked a court to halt certification and order an investigation if the margin suggested voter confusion could have affected the outcome. US District Judge Sharon Gleason in Anchorage dismissed the case on Sunday, finding Alaska could not conduct such a probe while preserving the secrecy of ballots.
Legal experts had said DOJ lacked authority to bring the case and risked appearing to favor the Republican incumbent.
“For the department to be trusted in its law enforcement decisions it has to ensure that people understand it does not take sides in political partisan disputes,” said Peter Keisler, acting attorney general under Republican President George W. Bush. “And this has not only the appearance but the evident reality of taking sides.”
Blanche has said the case sought to stop what he described as fraud by Daniel J. Sullivan, who denies trying to mislead voters. Peltola’s campaign said it had “no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.”
Asked about criticism of the lawsuit, a Justice Department official said at a press briefing on Thursday, “We bring lawsuits to enforce federal law.”
TRUMP ALLIES EMPOWERED
The Justice Department has traditionally proceeded cautiously in election investigations because its involvement can cause uncertainty or be exploited by candidates or political parties.
Its Public Integrity Section, staffed with career experts on election law, has often advised agents and prosecutors to wait until results are certified before intervening, according to former DOJ officials.
The Trump administration has slashed the size of the unit and suspended a requirement that federal prosecutors consult it on election-corruption probes. DOJ officials say US Attorney’s Offices are better positioned to decide whether charges are merited.
Instead, agents and prosecutors have been told that unresolved issues will be decided by Trump political appointees, according to three people familiar with the conversations.
The Deputy Attorney General’s Office will mediate disputes between agents and prosecutors, they said, a direct role that former DOJ officials said it has rarely played in election investigations.
Pels said “resolving disputes that can’t be resolved in the field is exactly the role that office exists to play.”

sources.news_title: Trump's California Ballot Fight Heads to Supreme Court Over Noncitizen Voting as Critics Warn of 'Chaos'
