Trump's California Ballot Fight Heads to Supreme Court Over Noncitizen Voting as Critics Warn of 'Chaos'
Nov. 2 2026, Published 2:35 p.m. ET
The Trump administration has taken its fight over roughly 20,000 California mail ballots to the U.S. Supreme Court, asking the justices to intervene one day before the Nov. 3 midterm election.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer filed an emergency application Monday after federal courts rejected the administration's efforts to force California election officials to set aside ballots from voters the government says are likely noncitizens.
The Justice Department wants those ballots held until the voters' citizenship can be verified.
California officials have challenged the federal list's reliability and argued that changing ballot procedures this late could disrupt the election and disenfranchise eligible voters.
Dispute Centers On Federal Voter List
The dispute began after the Department of Homeland Security and other federal agencies identified more than 20,000 California voters they considered likely noncitizens.
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit against California on Oct. 15, seeking an order requiring officials to separate ballots from people on the list and withhold them from counting until citizenship was confirmed.
Federal officials say they created the list by reviewing voter-registration information and federal immigration records. The administration argues that allowing potentially unlawful votes to be counted could dilute the votes of eligible citizens.
California, however, says the government has not established that the people on the list are actually ineligible voters.
Los Angeles County officials also raised questions about the data, saying a review of a sample found that some records belonged to inactive or canceled registrations and that some voters had reported being born in the United States.
The administration's request also came after California had already mailed ballots to its roughly 23 million registered voters beginning Oct. 1, as required under state law.
Lower Courts Reject Late Changes
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter rejected the Justice Department's request for emergency relief on Oct. 28.
Carter questioned the government's methodology and warned that forcing California to change its established election procedures so close to Election Day could disenfranchise eligible voters and disrupt the process.
The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals then ruled 2-1 against the administration on Oct. 30. Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez rejected the request, while Judge Patrick Bumatay dissented and argued that federal law supported the administration's position.
The appeals court majority said the requested relief could disenfranchise eligible voters and put the state's ballot-counting process in jeopardy.
California officials have also argued that separating the ballots at this stage would be extremely difficult because ballots are separated from their identifying envelopes during processing.
Supreme Court Faces Urgent Decision
Sauer's Supreme Court filing now asks the justices to step into the dispute as California's election process nears its final stage.
The case puts the court in the position of considering whether to require a major change to ballot handling immediately before Election Day.
The application was directed to Justice Elena Kagan, who handles emergency matters arising from the 9th Circuit, although she could refer the matter to the full court.
The administration argues that immediate action is necessary because ballots cannot be retrieved once they are processed and mixed with other votes.
California and its supporters counter that the government's proposed remedy would likely cause significant disruption.
Ballot Handling and Timing At Issue
The central question is no longer simply whether noncitizens are prohibited from voting in federal elections.
They are. The dispute is over whether the federal government has identified ineligible voters accurately enough, and whether courts should require California to change its established procedures at the last minute.
Noncitizen voting is illegal but rare, according to available audits and investigations.
The accuracy of the administration's California list remains contested, with federal officials defending their methodology and state officials arguing that it could incorrectly flag eligible voters.
The Supreme Court's response could determine whether California must take extraordinary steps involving thousands of disputed ballots just as voters head to the polls.

sources.news_title: Trump's election interference in California and Alaska prompts a series of judicial rebukes
sources.text:
Trump's Election Interference in California and Alaska Prompts a Series of Judicial Rebukes
Four federal courts say the Trump administration is trying to usurp the states' constitutional authority over elections.
The U.S. Constitution says "the times, places and manner of holding elections" for senators and representatives "shall be prescribed in each state by the legislature thereof," although Congress "may at any time by law make or alter such regulations." Yet in the run-up to Tuesday's elections, the Trump administration has unilaterally and repeatedly tried to impose its own restrictions on that constitutional power, resulting in a remarkable series of rebukes by federal courts, including four issued during the last five days.
In California, the Justice Department demanded that election officials segregate mail-in ballots from 20,000 voters it describes as "likely noncitizens." State and local officials declined to do so for several reasons.
California officials questioned the reliability of the Trump administration's list, which was produced by the Department of Homeland Security based on hazy, error-prone methods. They worried that the last-minute intervention would wreak havoc with ballot processing, deny residents mistakenly identified as noncitizens the right to vote, and violate a federal law that bars "any program the purpose of which is to systematically remove the names of ineligible voters from the official lists" within 90 days of an election.
In response, the Justice Department threatened to prosecute election workers for aiding and abetting violations of 18 USC 611, which makes it a misdemeanor for "any alien to vote" in a federal election. On Friday, Trina L. Thompson, a federal judge in San Francisco, issued a temporary restraining order (TRO) that says the Justice Department "shall not threaten, intimidate or coerce state or local elections officials or workers" who decline to "halt processing the ballots of any registered voter solely on the basis that the ballot belongs to an individual alleged by the Defendants to be ineligible to vote."
Thompson, a Joe Biden appointee, said her TRO is aimed at protecting "the freedom to exercise the right to vote free from threat, fear, or intimidation." She noted that "ballots have already been issued," that "Americans have already begun voting," and that election workers "have already begun processing ballots." Given "the consequences of inaction," she said, "the Court sees no reason to delay its ruling."
The Justice Department's threats "likely violated" the federal law against voter intimidation under color of law, Thompson said, and ran afoul of the Elections Clause. The Constitution, she noted, quoting the Supreme Court's 1972 decision in Roudebush v. Hartke, "reserves to the States the 'authority to provide a complete code for congressional elections, not only as to times and places, but in relation to notices, registration, supervision of voting, protection of voters, prevention of fraud and corrupt practices, counting of votes, duties of inspectors and canvassers, and making and publication of election returns.'"
In addition to threatening recalcitrant election officials with federal prosecution, the Justice Department sought a TRO compelling them to set aside the ballots of allegedly ineligible voters. David O. Carter, a federal judge in Santa Ana, rejected that application last Wednesday, saying the Trump administration's claims about unqualified voters were "not credible," especially given its pattern of dramatically downgrading its estimates of noncitizen voting in California and other states. On Friday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit declined to override Carter's decision.
"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," wrote Carter, a Bill Clinton appointee. "This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections. If Plaintiff's last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process. Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve."
The 9th Circuit had similar concerns. "We decline the United States's invitation to contravene the Elections Clause by undermining the Constitution's plain text," Judge Mark J. Bennett, a Donald Trump appointee, and Gabriel P. Sanchez, a Biden appointee, said in the per curiam opinion, from which Judge Patrick J. Bumatay, a Trump nominee, dissented. "If the United States believes different procedures are necessary for vote-by-mail ballots, we believe it should take that suggestion to Congress, not the courts."
The 9th Circuit added that "the potential violation" of the 90-day restriction on systematic purging of voter lists "provides an independent reason to conclude" that the Justice Department had not shown it was likely to prevail. "The United States effectively seeks to cancel (or potentially cancel) 'batches of registered voters based on a set procedure [which] is systematic as opposed to individualized,'" the appeals court said. "The consequence of the United States's request is not merely ballot segregation, but ultimately both the cancellation of the ballot and the removal of voters from the voting rolls."
The 9th Circuit also cited the Supreme Court's 2006 ruling in Purcell v. Gonzalez, which cautioned that judicial intervention close to an election can cause "voter confusion and consequent incentive to remain away from the polls." Purcell "counsels that we should not intervene at this late hour," the appeals court said. "The Purcell principle reflects the wisdom that we must not 'alter the election rules on the eve of an election,'" and it "'applies with even greater force' when, as here, an election is already underway."
California officials, "pursuant to their constitutional authority, established rules and
procedures to challenge a voter's ineligibility in the months directly preceding an
election," the 9th Circuit noted. "As the district court found—and we discern no clear error—there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system."
On Sunday, a federal judge in Alaska likewise cited Purcell in dismissing a Justice Department lawsuit that aimed to address potential voter confusion in that state's U.S. Senate race. The main choice in Alaska is between the incumbent senator, Daniel S. Sullivan, and his Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola. But the ranked-choice ballot also includes a freshly registered Republican, Daniel P. Sullivan, who was recruited by Peltola's campaign in the hope of drawing votes from the senator.
After Alaska's courts rejected efforts to bar Daniel P. Sullivan from the ballot, the Justice Department sought a court order that would apply only if the senator loses the election and his similarly named opponent receives enough votes to account for that outcome. If that happens, the Trump administration said, Alaska should not certify the results until "an investigation" can "determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
Since voters' choices are secret, it was not clear how such an investigation could possibly be conducted. "Requiring the segregation of ballots cast by voters for Daniel J. Sullivan so that these voters can be further investigated by law enforcement is not a remedy that this Court can or should order as it clearly violate Alaskans' right to a secret ballot," Sharon L. Gleason, chief judge of the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska, wrote in her decision on Sunday. "The relief requested here by the United States is 'infeasible.'"
Gleason, a Barack Obama appointee, added that Purcell "strongly cautions the Court against granting the relief the United States seeks." The Supreme Court, she noted, "has repeatedly emphasized that lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election."
The Trump administration argued that it was "not seeking to alter the time, place, or manner of Alaska's election," Gleason wrote. "Yet it seeks a court order preventing the State from certifying the election if certain circumstances occur; a court order requiring
the State to segregate and preserve certain ballots; and a court order permitting
the United States to conduct an investigation into the intent of those voters who
cast ballots for Daniel J. Sullivan. These requests certainly involve the time, place,
and manner of Alaska's election, which are the responsibilities of the State, not the
executive branch of the federal government."

sources.news_title: The Latest: Trump makes final midterm pitch as administration appeals to Supreme Court over ballots
sources.text:
President Donald Trump's administration appealed to the Supreme Court on Monday in its push to sideline thousands of disputed California mail ballots the day before the pivotal midterm elections. The emergency appeal came after an appeals court rejected the request to set aside some 20,000 ballots from people the federal government suspects may not be U.S. citizens.
Trumpclosed out the final weekend before Election Day with rallies in two states he had handily won in the past.
At the same time, Democrats began to fracture in Michigan, risking their effort to retake the Senate. Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers as Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election.
Trump made his closing pitch of the midterms Monday afternoon at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, pushing his slow, expensive and problem-plagued efforts to repair it back into the spotlight on the eve of Election Day.

US has conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, US official says
Iranian state television reported that explosions were heard on Qeshm Island. The official, who wasn’t authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said “Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets” had been targeted.
The strikes, which appeared to be limited as opposed to a full return to hostilities, came on the eve of crucial American midterm elections. Trump has previously said the U.S. wouldn’t launch strikes on Iran before the midterms.

U.S. Vice President JD Vance told reporters earlier Monday that he just spoke to Trump about talks with Iran and said “the president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement.”
— Michelle L. Price
‘It stinks,’ says Talarico supporter of the millions Musk spent against the Democrat
Bradley Hemmi stood near the back of Talarico’s final rally during a lull in the live music.
“It’s frustrating to see this state that’s so wealthy cut social services and cater to extremely wealthy people,” said Hemmi, adding that Elon Musk was chief among them.
The world’s richest man, and a Texas resident, appears to have sunk at least $158 million into supporting Talarico’s opponent, Republican Ken Paxton.
“It also represents the inequality when you have one man who can throw $150 million, or however many million it is, at one candidate,” he said.
Then, noting Musk has business dealings with the federal government, he added, “pretty corrupt.”
Big cheers for Haley Stevens at Rogers rally

Attendees chanted, “Haley! Haley! Haley!”

Many of Iowa’s Republican candidates close out campaign with Des Moines rally
A rain-soaked Ashley Hinson for Senate campaign bus drove into a ballroom in Des Moines, Iowa, as Fleetwood Mac’s “Don’t Stop” echoed across the room to remind a cheering crowd that no one can “stop thinking about tomorrow.”
Many of the Republicans on Iowa’s ticket took the stage for a final rally ahead of Tuesday’s election, including Hinson and U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, who touted “a record we are proud to stand behind.”
Nunn called his district, one of the most competitive in the country, the “tip of the spear” as Republicans battle to maintain their slim majority in the House.
Before introducing Hinson, Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley asked Iowans to give him a colleague who “won’t neutralize my vote.”
Hinson closed out the show flanked by her family, saying Iowa values are worth fighting for and “are on the ballot tomorrow.”
“Grab an umbrella,” Hinson said for those voting Tuesday. “At least it’s not a blizzard.”
Talarico voter likes that he welcomes Republicans into his movement
It’s been an ingredient of Talarico’s success as a Democrat running in the Republican bastion of Texas: a largely nonpartisan campaign that doesn’t malign the GOP.
Christina Edgar, a 52-year-old public health worker who attended Talarico’s final rally, says that’s why “he’s the first politician running that has given me hope.”
“With all the division coming out of the White House,” she continued, “I think it’s really important to have an open door.”
Edgar typically votes for Democrats, but Talarico will need Republican and independent voters to walk through that “open door” if he’s to find victory.
Sen. Darline Graham’s voice gives out as her campaign wraps up
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham’s voice has run out of steam as she wraps up her campaign in South Carolina.
The Republican spoke for barely more than a minute at the end of her four-month sprint after her brother, Lindsey Graham, died suddenly in July.
Polls have shown a tight race between Graham and Democratic pediatrician Annie Andrews. Andrews was at a get-out-the-vote rally in Charleston on Monday.
Darline Graham was appointed to her brother’s seat, then won a snap Republican primary. She’s struggled at times with the sudden public spotlight after years working in state government instead of politics.
In a raspy voice, Graham apologized twice and quickly introduced fellow Republican Alan Wilson, the attorney general running for governor.
“This is the final stop, and I have enjoyed every minute of it, and I promise you I will work so hard for this state every single day,” she said.
Talarico’s final rally is throbbing with energy and dance music
The outdoor amphitheater is packed with supporters and bars for libations, the trees above glow from blue lights, and the stage pumps dance music.
“This ain’t Texas, ain’t no hold ’em,” Beyoncé’s voice blares from the speakers.
With instruments waiting for a band onstage, it’s part concert, part final hurrah to end the long road to Election Day.
It’s a road that the crowd here hopes will end with James Talarico becoming the first Democrat in more than 30 years to win statewide in Texas.
No Election Day public appearances planned for Trump
His public schedule released by the White House shows the president participating in a series of private meetings, including a closed-door one with John Joseph Arrigo, the U.S. ambassador to Portugal.

Far from the campaign trail, Trump promotes his Reflecting Pool makeover before Election Day
President Trump stood silently Monday while triumphant music played as he held up a poster showing an image of the algae-clogged pool in front of the Lincoln Memorial.
It was the final moment of his last big speech before Election Day, far away from the campaign trail where Republicans were trying to make their case to voters to hang onto control of Congress.

In Virginia, House Speaker Mike Johnson says polls aren’t capturing GOP enthusiasm
GOP House Speaker Mike Johnson, rallying voters in a red-leaning Virginia congressional district with an unusually competitive contest this year, said Monday that polls suggesting Democrats have an edge in key congressional races aren’t registering Republican enthusiasm on the ground.

Trump hopes voters take note of plunging oil prices on Election Day
The president, during remarks at the Reflecting Pool, expressed hope that the American electorate would weigh Monday’s “plunge” in oil prices as they cast their ballots.
Oil prices dropped sharply on Monday amid renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war between the U.S. and Iran, now in its ninth month, that appeared to show signs of headway. Rising prices at the pump, a byproduct of the war, have loomed large over the midterm elections.
“I hope people realize that when they go into the voting booth, because we had to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon,” Trump said, remarking on the oil prices. “If we allowed Iran to have a nuclear weapon, this country could never function the same way.”
Brent crude was down about 7.5% on Monday, with a barrel trading around $104.98. That’s still far above the $70 mark it was trading at in the days before the war.
Washington, DC, voters can’t elect a voting member of Congress
Trump spent several minutes of his nearly hourlong closing pitch to voters highlighting his achievements cleaning up the nation’s capital, even though its residents have no voting representation in Congress.
Voters in the District of Columbia on Tuesday will elect a nonvoting delegate in the House, who can propose legislation and vote in committees but can’t vote on final legislation.
They’ll also elect two “shadow” senators and one “shadow” representative to lobby for statehood for the district.
Home to nearly 700,000, the city has more residents than Wyoming and Vermont.
Trump returned to the White House after the speech.
Trump says he plans to build a ‘promenade’ in DC
The president talked about his plans for building a triumphal arch and renovations for a public golf course, but also floated the idea of a “promenade” that would let people walk from the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac River.
“It’s a great architectural concept, simple and beautiful and white stone,” Trump said. He added that it hearkened back to the idea that the river would be the original entrance to the memorial, but the area had gotten “cluttered” with roadways and other projects.
Trump said he is also looking at lists of names for statues of historic figures that would be in a garden of heroes.
“We have a lot of great things planned for Washington,” Trump said, adding that he didn’t have the time to discuss all his plans for the country.
Trump pivots to the midterms after talking about DC renovations
After 20 minutes devoted to his D.C. construction projects, Trump said Tuesday’s elections could be the most important midterms “in our lifetime.”
The president tried to portray his political rivals as extremists, claiming that Democrats had “nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history.”
The Democrats have seen their chances of winning control of the House and Senate improve because of public frustration over Trump’s inability to bring down inflation and his decision to launch the Iran war.
But Trump cautioned that sitting presidents usually struggle in the midterm elections as he said the U.S. has its most secure borders and largest income tax cuts in the nation’s history.
“For some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms,” Trump said. “But we gave this a very strong shot.”
Electricity restored after outages in DC’s Foggy Bottom neighborhood
About 1,100 customers lost power earlier Monday after the city’s fire department said it was responding to reports of smoke coming from maintenance holes in the downtown Washington area.
Pepco, the electricity provider in Washington, is still investigating what caused the outage, spokesperson Jessica Babb said.
Power has been restored to all customers, she added.
Trump says the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool has reopened
In a speech to mark the reopening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool after repairs, Trump joked that he would rename it after himself.
The president is speaking about the troubled repairs to the pool, which he said was damaged by vandals despite an admission in court that shoddy renovations commissioned by Trump caused its shuttering.
The president has chosen this site to address voters on the final day before the Tuesday midterm elections.
Flooding in a Colorado tourist town is affecting Election Day voting plans
Flooding in the Southwest has forced a Colorado tourist town to alter its Election Day voting plans.
In Pagosa Springs, town residents impacted by the floods who haven’t voted yet can “visit any voter center across the state to request and receive a replacement ballot,” the Secretary of State’s office said in a news release.
People who cast in-person ballots outside their home county can vote only for statewide races, the office said. But if they have access to their mail ballot, they can return it to any drop box or voter center in the state by 7 p.m. on Election Day, and it will be sent to their county clerk for signature verification and tabulation, the office said.
Voting centers will still be open in La Plata County, but some county offices, including the clerk’s office, will have special hours on Tuesday.
Vance rallies in upstate New York as Election Day nears
Vice President JD Vance campaigned in rural upstate New York, disparaging Democrats as “lunatics” and warning that failing to elect Republicans could lead to a leftward swing for the country.
Speaking in an airport hangar in the town of Rome, Vance also touted Trump’s achievements, pointing to legislation he signed to end taxes on tips and overtime, even as the president’s approval ratings on the economy slipped to 25% last month.
He stumped for two Republicans running for Congress but did not talk about Bruce Blakeman, the Republican competing to unseat Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul.
Vance said voters could send a message to Democrats “that here in the New York 21st Congressional District, we are fighting for people who love the United States of America, not those who hate it.”
El-Sayed’s message to those worried about Stevens’ support of Rogers: ‘Go vote’
“If we’re nervous about where we’re going to go from here, go vote,” Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Monday at a campaign event in Ypsilanti.
El-Sayed spent the final day before the election campaigning alongside fellow Michigan Democrat Debbie Dingell and Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren.
Much of his speech focused on getting corporate money out of politics and establishing universal Medicare.
Haley Stevens, whom El-Sayed defeated in the August Democratic primary, endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday, exacerbating tensions among Democrats on the eve of the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.
Trump administration appeals to Supreme Court in push to sideline 20,000 California mail ballots
The Trump administration appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday in its push to sideline thousands of disputed California mail ballots the day before the pivotal midterm elections.
The emergency appeal came after an appeals court rejected the request to set aside some 20,000 ballots from people the federal government suspects may not be citizens. The Republican Trump administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite them being rare.
The federal government says those ballots should not be counted until the voters’ status can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.
A district court judge forcefully denied the Justice Department’s request and warned that the demand could disenfranchise citizens in the Nov. 3 midterm elections to determine control of Congress.
‘I’m learning what’s going on within our country, and this actually brought me out’
The stakes in Tuesday’s midterm elections are so high that Shane Dunn voted for the first time in his life, at age 65.
After a career as a cook up and down the East Coast, Dunn moved to the Philadelphia suburbs and voted last week in Levittown. “I was always a busy man,” he said outside his polling place. But now, “I’m learning what’s going on within our country, and this is actually what brought me out.”
Voters across the United States are getting their word in, too, as they determine which party controls the Senate and the House and takes charge of governors’ offices, legislatures and state leadership posts in the final two years of Trump’s presidency.
In dozens of Associated Press interviews with people who cast ballots at advance polling places or drop boxes across the country, the angst was palpable, most sharply from those who oppose Trump but also from many who support him.
Analysis: Republicans face a midterm reckoning of Trump’s making
For Trump, this week’s elections are about him. For his fellow Republicans, the risk is voters will agree.
Midterms almost always serve as a referendum on the president’s party, and losses typically ensue. But Trump’s decisions to impose tariffs, start a war and oversee extravagant Washington renovations — largely without congressional consultation — have made it harder for Republicans to navigate those historical headwinds.
There is a direct connection between his actions and higher gas prices, costlier groceries and persistently high inflation.
Republicans cannot blame the fallout from those decisions on past administrations when Trump has owned them so fulsomely. They also cannot easily distance themselves from an unpopular president who demands loyalty and routinely tells voters the economy is just fine.
At virtually every juncture before Election Day on Tuesday, Trump has complicated the task of protecting Republican majorities in Congress.
The Iran war is “making it exponentially harder for Republicans to keep the House and Senate,” Rep. Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin, one of the most vulnerable House Republicans, said in a debate while noting his support for the effort.

Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to block 20,000 California ballots
November 3, 2026
On the eve of the US midterm elections, the administration of President Donald Trump made a last ditch attempt to sideline over 20,000 mail-in ballots in California, claiming non-US citizens are attempting to vote.
The US Justice Department (DoJ), which is run by Trump's former personal attorney Todd Blanche, has claimed to have a list documenting non-US citizens on California's voter rolls.
In mid October, the federal government first filed a lawsuit based on the allegations, which was rejected by a California district court.
On Monday, the DoJ asked for a "limited injunction" directing the state of California to "stop commingling suspected illegal ballots with legal ones" pending the verification of voters' status.
However, hours after the appeal was filed, the Supreme Court said it would decline to stop California from counting the votes.
When the initial lawsuit was filed by the Trump administration earlier in October, Los Angeles District Judge David Carter had warned that singling out ballots would "wreak havoc" on the election process and harm voters' trust in the democratic process.
"If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," Carter wrote in rejecting the initial suit.
Early voting has been underway in California for several weeks, with hundreds of thousands of ballots already processed.
Analysis shows thousands of eligible voters on ballot blacklist
The voter list had been compiled by the US Department of Homeland Security. In its response to the federal government's lawsuit, California defended its election integrity, and said the process used by the Trump administration to identify non-citizen voters was likely flawed and full of errors.
Last week, another federal judge ordered the DoJ to share its list with an immigrant rights group, and a voting rights watchdog based out of the University of California Los Angeles (UCLA).
A legal filing of the analysis found that thousands of US citizens on the list appear to be inexplicably flagged as ineligible to vote. US District Judge Carter said people recently flagged as noncitizens on voter rolls in other states have repeatedly turned out to be naturalised US citizens.
Trump's fixation on voter fraud
Trump has made unfounded claims of election fraud for years, despite multiple investigations finding such malfeasance is exceedingly rare.
For the current midterm election cycle, Trump has zeroed in on claiming non US citizens are trying to vote, despite these claims being repeatedly debunked by research and investigation.
"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch," US District Judge Carter wrote in October.
The most populous US state, California, leans heavily Democratic, and is not expected to be a competitive state for Trump's Republicans in the midterms.
California governor Gavin Newsom is an outspoken critic of Trump, and has warned the president's administration against trying to interfere in the state's voting process.
Ahead of the midterm voting on Tuesday, Newsom announced the deployment of election law experts, poll observers and a help line for voters to report any attempts of intimidation or interference at the polls.

“The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied.”

John Sauer in his now-rejected Supreme Court application.

November 3 is election day across the US for midterm elections, and questions have been raised about election and voting integrity in many jurisdictions. sources.text:
Supreme Court rejects Trump request to set aside California ballots
Top court declines to block California from counting ballots of voters Trump administration claims are not US citizens.
The United States Supreme Court has declined to intervene on behalf of President Donald Trump’s administration in its bid to force California not to count the ballots of more than 20,000 voters it claims are not citizens.
The Department of Justice had filed an emergency request earlier in the day, just one day before the US midterm elections. It is the latest development in a legal battle between the administration and California, a Democratic stronghold and the most populous US state.
California says the move could disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters.
The Justice Department wanted the Supreme Court to step in immediately and force California to set aside ballots from voters who appear on a list compiled by the Department of Homeland Security until their citizenship status can be verified.
The department argues that once the ballots are mixed in with others, there would be no way to identify and remove them if the voters were later found to be ineligible.
But California says the list is unreliable and could include thousands of US citizens.
Voting has been under way since early October, with ballots mailed to about 23 million registered voters and hundreds of thousands already processed. State officials say it would be nearly impossible to separate the ballots in question.
Last week, a federal judge rejected the administration’s request, raising concerns about the reliability of the data on the US Department of Homeland Security’s list.
“If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” Judge David Carter wrote.
The administration turned to the Supreme Court after a federal appeals court also rejected the request on Friday.
In September, the Supreme Court rejected an earlier effort to restrict mail-in voting.
The dispute comes as Republicans fight to retain control of the US Congress in Tuesday’s elections.
Trump has repeatedly made false claims about widespread voter fraud, but studies and state audits have shown that ineligible voting, including by non-citizens, is rare.

DOJ Asks Supreme Court to Take Action on California Ballot Demands
sources.text:
On the eve of Election Day, the Justice Department Monday asked the U.S. Supreme Court to weigh in and stop California election officials from counting more than 20,000 ballots from people the federal government suspects may be non-citizens.
The request comes after a split 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals panel and a Los Angeles federal judge last week rejected the DOJ’s attempt to obtain a temporary restraining order separating the allegedly ineligible vote-by-mail ballots.
The 2-1 vote Friday by the appeals panel was the latest setback for the administration’s efforts to assert control over state-run elections.
“We decline the United States’ invitation to contravene the Elections Clause by undermining the Constitution’s plain text,” the majority wrote in its decision.
In a forceful opinion last week, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter said the federal government’s request “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens.”
The judge set an expedited hearing for Nov. 13 in Los Angeles federal court to further explore the matter. Carter said election officials have until Dec. 3 — the date by which election results must be certified — to resolve the issue, suggesting there was no need for an emergency injunction.
Carter indicated he would call witnesses to determine the reliability of the methodology and data that prosecutors used in creating the list of 20,000 possible non-citizens. He said previously that federal officials provided only vague explanations “and raised multiple questions regarding reliability” of the process.
In asking for a quick ruling on the renewed motion, the DOJ wrote that “once a vote-by-mail ballot has been processed, it cannot be undone if it is later determined that the voter was ineligible.”
The DOJ filed a notice Monday that it plans to appeal to the high court. The Supreme Court could act on the petition at any time, but there is no deadline.
The midterm elections are crucial because they will determine which parties hold majorities in both chambers of Congress.
Carter, a Bill Clinton appointee who is overseeing the closely watched lawsuit, United States of America v. State of California, et al., previously dismissed a DOJ attempt to force California to turn over its full voter registration list to the federal government.
The Justice Department has sued 30 states that refused to turn over voter data, losing the majority of the cases so far.
The federal government sued California on Oct. 15, more than a week after mail ballots were sent to all registered voters, demanding it set aside 20,000 ballots from alleged non-citizens after the state refused to voluntarily sequester those votes.
In opposition to the administration’s demand for an injunction, the defendants — Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan — argued they lack the mechanisms and legal authority to freeze mail ballots until voters’ citizenship can be verified.
The DOJ’s first appeal to the 9th Circuit was denied because the lower court judge had not yet ruled on the request. The three-judge appellate panel quickly rebuffed the effort following a rare weekend hearing.
In his subsequent ruling, Carter wrote that by moving to have ballots sequestered, the Trump administration embarked on “a broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference.”
On Thursday, federal prosecutors pursued subpoenas of California state and local election officials in connection with alleged illegal voting in the midterm elections.
“The President of the United States has a loose grip on the law and an even looser grip on reality,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta posted on X on Saturday. “As I’ve said many times, the only election Donald Trump recognizes as valid is one where he wins. There is no widespread voter fraud. The federal government has no right to interfere in California’s elections.”

sources.news_title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to intervene in California ballots dispute
sources.text:
The Trump administration on Monday morning asked the Supreme Court to intervene in its efforts to keep California from counting ballots cast by what it contends are more than 20,000 noncitizens who have registered to vote in that state. In a brief, unsigned order released to reporters shortly before 6 p.m., however, the court turned down the government's request. There were no noted dissents.
In a 19-page filing, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer requested an order from the justices that would require California to keep those ballots separate until the voters’ citizenship could be verified. “Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones,” Sauer wrote, “there is no way to get the challenged ballots back.”
The filing was the latest chapter in the Trump administration’s push to combat alleged voter fraud. It began last month, when the administration went to federal court in Los Angeles, seeking an order directing the state not to send ballots to, or count the ballots of, voters who were likely not citizens.
On Oct. 28, U.S. District Judge David Carter turned down the government’s request for a temporary order directing California to sequester the ballots of “likely noncitizens.” Among other things, he questioned the credibility of the Trump administration’s allegations that the voters it had identified were not U.S. citizens. On Friday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit also rejected the Trump administration’s motion for emergency relief.
With the midterm elections now just one day away, the Trump administration sought relief next in the Supreme Court. Sauer argued that the government is likely to prevail on the merits of its claim – a key factor that courts consider in deciding whether to grant temporary relief – because federal law bars anyone who is not a U.S. citizen from voting in federal elections. Therefore, he wrote, “it follows that any ballot cast by an alien is unlawful” and states cannot count them.
The United States will also suffer permanent harm (another factor that courts consider in deciding whether to award temporary relief), Sauer continued, because “‘California admits that there is no way to trace a ballot after it is processed.’” The government’s “injury will continue to mount,” Sauer contended, “through Tuesday, November 10 (a week after election day, California’s deadline for receiving mail ballots.)”
By contrast, Sauer said, California will not suffer “undue hardship” from having to sequester the ballots at issue in this case. Indeed, he suggested, “California’s own election laws contemplate the segregation of challenged ballots, and the segregation of challenged ballots is a standard remedy in election cases.”
Sauer asked the court to also issue an immediate temporary order, known as an administrative injunction, “that requires California to segregate mail ballots from persons whom the United States has identified as likely noncitizens” while the justices consider the government’s request.
The Trump administration’s filing went first to Justice Elena Kagan, who has primary responsibility for emergency appeals from the 9th Circuit. Kagan then referred it to the full court, which declined the Trump administration’s request.

Day before election, Trump’s DOJ asks US Supreme Court to rule in California voting case
The U.S. Department of Justice logo is displayed on a speaker’s podium. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)
The U.S. Department of Justice on Monday asked the U.S. Supreme Court to require California to set aside the ballots of suspected noncitizen voters in a last-ditch appeal by the Trump administration to exert control over the state’s vote counting.
The request came on the eve of Election Day and as more than 5 million mail ballots have already been cast in California, a state where voters are expected to elect dozens of Democrats to the U.S. House.
California’s election could be thrown into chaos if the Supreme Court grants the request. State and local election officials have previously warned that they have no easy way to quickly identify and set aside the ballots of individuals on the list.
In the Trump administration’s emergency application, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer noted that federal law prohibits voting by noncitizens, who still do sometimes vote “despite that prohibition,” he wrote.
“Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back,” Sauer added.
Logistically difficult
As a universal vote-by-mail state, every voter in California is sent a mail ballot. While millions of these ballots have already been returned, millions more may be dropped off on Tuesday or arrive by mail in the coming days.
Aman Bhullar, an assistant Los Angeles County registrar-recorder/county clerk, warned in a court declaration in October that the Trump administration’s request could wreak havoc on elections.
“The potential consequences of implementing DOJ’s demand are severe and range from halting all counting; halting in-person voters’ ability to cast votes; or otherwise interfering with the ability to accurately count votes,” Bhullar wrote.
Already a week ago, Shelby Wayment, staff attorney at the University of California, Los Angeles Safeguarding Democracy Project, questioned the feasibility of the DOJ’s demands. Ballots have already been mailed out and were being processed, she said.
“Just logistically, I don’t think it’s possible at this point,” Wayment said in a late October interview.
No widespread fraud
The Justice Department sued California in October, alleging that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security had identified 20,000 suspected noncitizen voters. California officials raised concerns about the veracity of the list, and declined to take action based on it.
An immigrant rights group, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, has raised serious concerns about the list after a judge forced the Trump administration to share a copy with the organization.
The group said in a court filing Saturday that an analysis by data experts found that 42% of the names weren’t found on California’s current voter file. At least 22 names on the list match names of U.S. citizens compiled by the organization, the analysis found.
“There is no widespread voter fraud. The federal government has no right to interfere in California’s elections,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said in a statement on Saturday.
11th hour challenge
The Justice Department has said the Department of Homeland Security compiled the list by checking a public copy of California’s voter file against federal records and information from the research service Lexis Nexis.
A district court judge and the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals have both ruled against the Trump administration in the case. State and local officials have argued the Justice Department exceeded its authority because states administer elections under the U.S. Constitution.
Even though the 9th Circuit issued a decision on Friday, the Justice Department didn’t ask the Supreme Court to intervene until midday Monday, less than 24 hours before Election Day.
The Justice Department has asked for an administrative stay that would require California to begin segregating ballots of voters on the list while the Trump administration prepares a full appeal. While it’s unknown how the Supreme Court will rule, in general the justices frown on federal courts ordering major last-minute changes to elections.
Because the case arises out of the 9th Circuit, Justice Elena Kagan, one of the court’s three liberals, will be the first to review the application.
Walter Olsen, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute’s Robert A. Levy Center for Constitutional Studies, in a statement predicted the Supreme Court will reject the request. He argued that the Justice Department is asking California officials to violate their own state laws.
“The Supreme Court should and I believe will reject the administration’s nervy last-minute attempts to meddle in California’s elections, as lower courts have rejected them,” Olsen said.

sources.text:
Supreme Court denies DOJ request to intervene in California ballot case
DOJ asked justices for an emergency order to set aside ballots
The Supreme Court on Monday denied a request from the Justice Department to intervene in its effort to have California set aside the ballots of 20,000 voters who the Trump administration argues could be noncitizens who illegally cast votes.
The unanimous, unexplained order came hours after the DOJ made the request and just before the votes are counted in the midterm elections. It was the latest maneuver in the fast-moving, high-profile effort by the administration to insert itself in state voting procedures. The application asked the justices for an emergency order for the state to set aside those ballots until the voters’ citizenship could be determined.
“In this case, this Office is informed that the Executive Branch has identified over 20,000 individuals who appear to be registered to vote in California based on publicly accessible information and who, based on the Executive Branch’s review, are likely not U.S. citizens,” the application said.
The request followed a ruling by a federal judge in California that the lawsuit likely violated several civil rights laws and improperly inserted the federal government in state election procedures.
A separate panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit turned aside an appeal of that ruling Friday.
The Justice Department filed the lawsuit last month, days after state officials had refused to take a flash drive the administration said included the names of the purported noncitizens. The DOJ argued that it had compiled the 20,000 names of alleged noncitizens and that state officials should impose additional requirements before allowing their votes to be counted.
State officials have argued that there is no federal role in the state election and that there was no evidence the voters had actually returned ballots or weren’t citizens.
The application came amid multiple last-minute efforts from the Trump administration to weigh in on state election processes, including a similar letter to Washington state officials and a lawsuit seeking to delay the certification of the Alaska Senate contest due to the presence of two similarly named candidates on the ballot.
The Trump administration has more broadly sought to assert a greater federal role in state authority over elections, dovetailing with President Donald Trump’s evidence-free claims of widespread voter fraud. The push started shortly after Trump began his second term, with an executive order seeking to require proof of citizenship to vote nationwide. That order was largely stopped by the courts.
Separately, the Justice Department sought private records of voters across dozens of states, another effort that was rejected by the courts.
Additionally, earlier this year Trump issued an executive order seeking to curb mail voting nationwide and force states to provide mail officials with lists of eligible voters. That was also stopped by the Supreme Court.

Election Eve: Trump Asks Supreme Court to Set Aside CA Ballots
sources.text:
The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to order California to set aside the mail ballots of more than 20,000 voters the Justice Department says may not be citizens, bringing the government's most contested pre-election lawsuit to the justices one day before the midterm elections that will decide control of Congress. The emergency application, filed by Solicitor General D. John Sauer and directed to Justice Elena Kagan, who handles matters from the 9th Circuit, came after a federal district judge and a divided appeals panel both refused the request, with the 9th Circuit warning on Friday that there was "no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system." "That doomsday prediction ignores that segregating ballots is a routine remedy when the lawfulness of ballots is questioned," Sauer wrote.
The filing landed on the day the president had set aside for a different kind of closing argument. Speaking from behind ballistic glass at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Monday afternoon, with a banner reading "Back, and more beautiful than ever!" and the Washington Monument behind him, Trump spent the first 20 minutes of his final scheduled remarks on the pool itself, holding up printed photographs of its condition before the repairs, describing fountain restorations around the capital, graffiti removal on the National Mall and the new White House helipad, and declaring the project "a complete job" of which "we're very proud." "This is a massive piece of pool," he said. Only then did he turn to Tuesday. "We've got some big races tomorrow. I guess some of the voting has already gone on, but tomorrow is election day," he said, telling Republicans that "we gave this very strong shot." He tacked on a claim that tariffs had created "trillions of dollars" in wealth, and left. It was the last of a month in which he held 28 rallies, the final one Sunday night in Salina, Kansas, where he told the crowd he had "never worked the midterms like I have this one" and that he felt "a little bit" nostalgic about what might be his last. "I'm closing the sucker down," he said. His closing poll numbers were less sentimental: NBC News' final survey put his approval at 40 percent, with respondents expressing dissatisfaction with their personal finances for the first time in the poll's 30-year history, a polling average cited by MS NOW put it at 35.6, more than 54 million Americans had already voted, and a senior administration official described the mood inside the White House as one of "resignation" ahead of expected losses.
The venue was itself an argument. The pool reopened last week after a renovation that Trump promised in April would take days and cost about $1.5 million, and that instead ran to roughly $14 million, required the pool to be drained again in July, and produced a vandalism prosecution that a judge permanently dismissed; Trump, who repeated on Sunday that the pool "was vandalized badly," said last month that U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro had "folded like an umbrella" in the case. Asked why he was closing the campaign there rather than in a battleground state, he said: "just to show how beautiful it is." He also told a podcast this weekend that he would "love to run again" but acknowledged the Constitution's language on a third term is "very exacting."
The California case is the sharpest edge of a broader effort. The Justice Department sued the state and the Los Angeles County registrar last month after producing a list of about 20,000 registered voters it says federal records flag as possible noncitizens, and demanded that any ballot they returned be held uncounted until citizenship was verified. California called the list "highly suspect," said it already had safeguards against noncitizen voting, and argued the list likely swept in many citizens. The district judge agreed and said the demand risked disenfranchising eligible voters; the 9th Circuit panel split 2–1, with Judge Patrick Bumatay in dissent calling the government's request reasonable. The administration has lost three such fights in a week: a federal judge in Washington state barred prosecutors from threatening election workers, and on Sunday a judge in Alaska dismissed the department's suit to block certification of the Senate race there. Gov. Gavin Newsom warned judges over the weekend to be ready for possible attempts to seize ballots. Whether the Supreme Court acts before polls close, or at all, was unknown on Monday evening; a request to Kagan can be referred to the full court, and the justices have in past cycles been reluctant to change election procedures on the eve of a vote. Kagan had set no deadline for California's response by Monday evening, and the state said more than 6.4 million ballots had already been cast and were being counted. In a separate ruling the same day, a fourth federal court found the administration was exceeding its powers in trying to force the state to segregate ballots from the list. "If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," Judge David Carter wrote.
In Michigan, the day's other surprise came from the Democratic side. Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed the Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, on Sunday, and in a tense interview with CNN's Anderson Cooper on Monday declined to say directly why she had abandoned her party's candidate. The endorsement infuriated Democrats, who need the open seat to have a path to a Senate majority, and handed Republicans a closing-weekend story in a race that has turned on gas prices and on attacks by Trump and Vice President JD Vance on El-Sayed's Muslim faith. Stevens said Monday she "absolutely" wanted Democrats to win the Senate but stood by the endorsement, citing a "very painful" ad she said told Democrats like her the party had no room for them; El-Sayed said his campaign had nothing to do with it. Trump's reaction was shorter: "We'd love to have her!"
Vance spent the eve of the election in Ohio and upstate New York, where he campaigned in Rome for Anthony Constantino, a Trump-backed House candidate whose recorded songs include one calling New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani a terrorist. Vance labeled the Democratic candidate "Blake Gende-Biden," told the crowd that Democrats wanted to show "even here in beautiful upstate New York, the communists can win," and joined chants of "ditch the witch" directed at Gov. Kathy Hochul. He said Monday was his last day on the trail.
The map the two parties will wake to on Tuesday is one in which Democrats are favored to retake the House and are competitive in enough Senate seats, Michigan, Alaska, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Maine among them, to make a four-seat net gain conceivable if the night breaks their way. Trump has said he will accept the results "if they're honest elections," and the administration's lawsuits in California, Alaska and Washington state are the clearest guide to what that qualification means: the government has sought, in each, a mechanism to hold or inspect ballots after the fact, and in each a court has so far refused.
What remains for Tuesday is the counting, and the question of how quickly the administration moves from litigation before the vote to litigation about it. California's 20,000 ballots will be counted unless the Supreme Court says otherwise. Alaska's will be, too, with a ranked-choice tabulation that will not finish for weeks. The president closed his campaign at a monument to a predecessor who won a wartime election he was not sure he would win; the glass between him and the Reflecting Pool was a reminder of the year that preceded this one, and the filing at the Supreme Court a reminder that the campaign's last argument is being made to nine justices as much as to the voters.

**UPDATE 6:00 PM: SCOTUS has denied the DOJ’s request to force California to set aside 20,000 ballots suspected to have gone to noncitizens.
BREAKING: The Supreme Court denied the Trump administration's emergency request to force California to set aside mail-in ballots from roughly 20,000 suspected noncitizens until their citizenship could be verified, one day before the midterm elections. pic.twitter.com/hjQzYV7Ht3
— SCOTUS Wire (@scotus_wire) November 2, 2026
**Previous reporting….
The Department of Justice has asked the Supreme Court for an administrative injunction to force California to set aside 20,000 ballots for suspected noncitizens.
“This Court should issue an injunction, pending the United States’ appeal to the Ninth Circuit and any subsequent proceedings in this Court, that requires California to segregate mail ballots from persons whom the United States has identified as likely noncitizens,” wrote Solicitor General D. John Sauer. “The Court should also enter an administrative injunction to that effect while it considers this application.”
Justice Elena Kagan handles matters concerning the 9th Circuit. She can respond alone or refer the decision to the full court.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit rejected the DOJ’s request on Friday, saying the DOJ “failed to meet its burden in showing that an injunction pending appeal is warranted.”
“Major concerns remain that granting the United States’s requested relief might result in immense hardship to Defendants and harm the public interest by risking the disenfranchisement of eligible voters and putting the entire tabulation process in jeopardy,” wrote Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez.
Judge Patrick Bumatay dissented, reminding everyone that the move “would not cancel any vote but would allow time to verify the eligibility of suspected noncitizens.”
The DOJ sued California on October 16 after the state did not review a list of possible noncitizens who would automatically receive federal election ballots.
“We provided California an opportunity to self correct its records and we requested that it segregate the suspected illegal ballots for the upcoming election,” Attorney General Todd Blanche wrote on X. “California has refused to comply and intends to facilitate noncitizens in voting, which is a violation of federal law.”
The lawsuit says Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) performed its duties, leading agents to “reasonably” believe California has 20,000 noncitizens registered to vote.
The DOJ sent Los Angeles County “a password-protected thumb drive identifying people they believe are likely noncitizens who were sent mail-in ballots.”
Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder/county clerk for Los Angeles County, claimed “he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device and hasn’t yet accessed any files.”
However, in a declaration opposing any stoppage of ballot counting, officials offered conflicting statements.
One woman said the registrar’s office lacked the equipment to verify voter citizenship.
Yet, one guy admitted his team “conducted a preliminary analysis” of 200 records from the list the feds sent them.

sources.text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The Trump administration asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday to intervene in its fight with California over more than 20,000 voters the Justice Department says may be noncitizens, seeking an emergency order requiring their mail ballots to be separated one day before Election Day.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the justices to prevent the disputed ballots from being mixed with other votes while litigation continues. The government argues that once ballots are removed from identifying envelopes and counted, any ballot later found to have been cast by an ineligible voter could no longer be isolated.
The Justice Department says federal immigration records identified roughly 20,000 people who are “likely” noncitizens and may also be registered California voters. However, both citizenship and voter-registration status remain disputed, and the government has acknowledged that additional investigation is needed.
California has challenged both the accuracy of the list and the Justice Department’s legal authority to demand that ballots be segregated. A federal district judge rejected the government’s request, and the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to intervene in a 2-1 decision, warning that last-minute ballot restrictions could disenfranchise eligible voters and disrupt an election already underway.
Questions about the list’s accuracy have become central to the dispute. An analysis submitted by the UCLA Voting Rights Project found that 8,880 of 20,930 names — about 42% — could not be matched to California’s voter file. Researchers also identified at least 22 confirmed U.S. citizens and said thousands of naturalized citizens may have been incorrectly flagged. WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration appealed to the Supreme Court on Monday in its push to sideline thousands of disputed California mail ballots the day before the pivotal midterm elections.
The emergency appeal came after a divided appeals court rejected the request to set aside some 20,000 ballots from people the federal government suspects may not be citizens.
The federal government says those ballots should not be counted until the voters’ status can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.
The Republican Trump administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite them being rare.
A district court judge forcefully denied the Justice Department's request and warned that the demand could disenfranchise citizens in Tuesday's midterm elections to determine control of Congress.
The Justice Department asked the high court for a “limited injunction” that would direct California to set aside the ballots while the case plays out.
“Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote.
Voting has been underway in California, a largely Democratic state, since early October. All of the state’s roughly 23 million registered voters are mailed a ballot. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. California election officials have said that finding and setting aside the challenged ballots now would be logistically impossible.
Lower courts have sided with the state, with a district judge warning that segregating ballots would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections and erode trust in the democratic process.
“If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” wrote U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who was nominated by President Bill Clinton, a Democrat.
A 2-1 appeals court panel upheld his order, with one judge appointed by Trump and another appointed by President Joe Biden, a Democrat, voting in favor. The third judge on the panel, also appointed by Trump, argued in a dissent that California’s unwillingness to separate the ballots encourages the “violation of federal law.”
The Justice Department has sought to move the case along quickly, unsuccessfully asking an appeals court to intervene early.
Trump's administration has racked up a series of wins in emergency appeals before the Supreme Court in his second term, but the justices previously rejected the president’s push to restrict mail ballots ahead of the midterms.
