sources.news_title: DOJ Takes California Ballot Dispute to Supreme Court, Seeks to Block 20,000 Votes Pending Citizenship Checks
sources.text:
The Trump administration filed an emergency Supreme Court appeal one day before the midterm elections, asking justices to require California to set aside approximately 20,000 mail ballots from voters suspected of being noncitizens after lower federal courts rejected the request.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
WASHINGTON — The Justice Department asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday, Nov. 2, to intervene in California’s midterm elections and prevent approximately 20,000 mail-in ballots from being counted until election officials verify the voters’ citizenship, escalating a legal dispute over voter eligibility just one day before Americans head to the polls.
The emergency application followed multiple defeats in federal courts, where judges rejected the Trump administration’s argument that California should be compelled to separate ballots associated with individuals federal investigators identified as potentially ineligible to vote.
According to an Associated Press report published Monday, the Justice Department wants the Supreme Court to order California officials to preserve the disputed ballots separately from other votes until citizenship verification can be completed.
Federal prosecutors argue that allowing the ballots to be processed and counted alongside those of other voters could make it impossible to identify and remove any unlawful votes later.
California officials dispute the accuracy of the federal government’s list, warning that the proposed intervention could prevent eligible U.S. citizens from having their ballots counted and disrupt an election already underway.
The dispute began Oct. 15, when the Justice Department filed a lawsuit against California, alleging that federal investigators had identified more than 20,000 registered voters who were likely noncitizens.
The department said Homeland Security investigators compared publicly available California voter registration records with federal immigration information to identify individuals whose eligibility warranted further investigation.
Under California law, ballots are mailed to all active registered voters, meaning people identified in the federal review could already have received ballots for the Nov. 3 election.
Attorney General Todd Blanche accused state officials of failing to address possible unlawful voting.
“State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America,” Blanche said when announcing the lawsuit.
He argued that knowingly allowing ineligible individuals to vote could undermine confidence in election results.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also defended the federal investigation, emphasizing that noncitizens are prohibited from voting in federal elections.
The Justice Department initially demanded that California officials examine the identified registrations and ensure any ballots returned by those individuals were not counted until their citizenship could be established.
California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Attorney General Rob Bonta challenged the federal government’s allegations and questioned the reliability of its screening methods.
State officials said the department had not provided sufficient underlying information to establish that the identified individuals were ineligible.
California also argued that the demand would require substantial changes to established election procedures shortly before voting concluded.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter rejected the administration’s request for emergency relief Oct. 28.
In his ruling, Carter warned that forcing the state to separate the ballots based on unverified citizenship allegations could interfere with lawful voting and create confusion among election workers.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Carter wrote, according to ABC News’ coverage of the ruling.
The judge also cautioned that the proposed order could interfere with the voting rights of eligible citizens.
California officials welcomed the ruling, arguing that the administration had failed to establish a legal basis for the requested restrictions.
Bonta said the Justice Department’s list potentially included eligible voters and that federal authorities had not supplied the information necessary to confirm their status.
In an Oct. 28 statement, the California attorney general said the proposed measures threatened to undermine voting rights and disrupt an election already in progress.
The case also reached the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, where judges rejected attempts by the administration to obtain emergency relief.
An earlier appeal was dismissed because the appellate court determined that it lacked jurisdiction to intervene before the district court ruled.
Following Carter’s decision, the Justice Department again sought appellate intervention.
A divided three-judge panel rejected that request Oct. 30, leaving the lower court’s ruling in place.
The administration subsequently turned to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to intervene before Election Day.
Federal prosecutors maintain that their requested remedy is limited because it would preserve the disputed ballots while determining whether the individuals who submitted them are legally eligible to vote.
California officials argue that separating ballots based on an unverified federal list could effectively deny thousands of citizens the right to participate.
The dispute also involves the distinction between suspected noncitizen registrations and confirmed unlawful voting.
A voter registration record flagged by a federal database does not necessarily establish that the person is a noncitizen.
Immigration records can become outdated when individuals become naturalized citizens, and administrative discrepancies can produce incorrect matches.
Los Angeles County officials reported that a preliminary review of 200 names from the federal list identified a substantial number of individuals who reported being born in the United States.
Officials also found that many people in the sample had no voting history.
Those findings have contributed to questions about the reliability of the government’s broader allegations.
Federal law generally prohibits noncitizens from voting in elections for president or Congress, and violations can result in criminal penalties.
However, states are responsible for administering elections under constitutional and statutory requirements, including procedures for registering voters, checking eligibility and counting ballots.
The Justice Department argues that federal prohibitions against noncitizen voting justify intervention when state procedures allegedly allow unlawful ballots to be counted.
California maintains that the federal government cannot compel election officials to alter voting procedures based on unproven allegations without satisfying the applicable legal requirements.
The Supreme Court’s consideration of the emergency application comes as voting has already been underway in California for several weeks.
The state has approximately 23 million registered voters, and hundreds of thousands of mail ballots have already been processed.
California’s extensive mail-voting system allows ballots to be returned before Election Day, while eligible ballots postmarked by Election Day can be accepted under applicable state deadlines.
Changing the treatment of ballots during that process could impose new responsibilities on county election administrators, including identifying specific voters, locating their returned ballots and conducting additional eligibility checks.
The timing is central to the dispute because federal courts have long expressed concern about changing election rules immediately before voting.
The Supreme Court has previously cautioned against late judicial interventions that could confuse voters or disrupt election administration, a principle commonly associated with its 2006 decision in Purcell v. Gonzalez.
The Justice Department argues that protecting federal elections from unlawful voting requires immediate action despite those concerns.
California officials contend that the administration has not demonstrated that the alleged problem justifies overriding established election procedures.
The case arrives amid broader disagreements between the Trump administration and Democratic-led states over voter registration records, federal oversight and election security requirements.
The Justice Department has also pursued citizenship-related voter registration inquiries in other states, including Washington, where officials were asked to examine several hundred individuals identified as possible noncitizens.
State officials have questioned the accuracy of some federal data and warned against removing voters without adequate verification.
The California dispute is particularly significant because of its timing and the size of the state’s congressional delegation.
All 52 California House seats are on the ballot Tuesday, along with statewide and local contests.
Although the disputed ballots represent a small fraction of the state’s registered electorate, individual congressional races can be decided by narrow margins.
The Justice Department has not established that the approximately 20,000 registrations under review represent 20,000 unlawful votes, and the Supreme Court has not determined that the identified voters are ineligible.
The administration’s emergency application seeks to preserve the ability to exclude ballots if citizenship checks subsequently establish that they were unlawfully cast.
California’s position is that eligible voters should not have their ballots set aside based on unverified allegations.
As of Monday, the Supreme Court had not issued a ruling on the emergency request.
The justices’ decision will determine whether California can continue processing the disputed ballots under its existing procedures or must implement additional restrictions immediately before the midterm elections.
The outcome could also influence how courts evaluate federal demands for last-minute election interventions when questions about voter eligibility remain unresolved.

sources.news_title: Trump’s Efforts to Rig the Midterms Have Failed In Court—So Far
sources.text:
President Donald Trump has had a stressful midterm elections season. Opinion polling shows that a whopping 60 percent of Americans disapprove of the standard-bearer of the Republican Party. The GOP is widely expected to lose its majority in the House of Representatives. And Senate seats once considered Republican strongholds now look more like toss-ups. The New York Times reports that the “mood” in the White House is “grim.”
The last time Trump was in the White House and unhappy with the results of an election, he abused the power of the White House in efforts to set those election results aside. Following his defeat in 2020, Trump directed the Department of Justice to conduct sham election crime investigations, pressure state officials to replace legitimate electoral votes with votes for him, and otherwise lean on states to alter election results and keep him in power. 
A federal grand jury indicted Trump for this conduct, but in July 2024, the Republican majority on the Supreme Court shut down the attempt to hold him criminally responsible. Chief Justice John Roberts downplayed Trump’s conscription of DOJ attorneys into service as election saboteurs, characterizing the scheme as mere “discussions with Justice Department officials.” In Trump v. United States, Roberts reasoned that deciding which crimes should be investigated and prosecuted is a “quintessentially executive function,” and he concluded that presidents are “absolutely immune from criminal prosecution” for conduct that falls within their “exclusive sphere of constitutional authority.”
Fast forward to November 2026, and Trump is again facing rejection at the ballot box. So, armed with Roberts’s blessing, Trump has again weaponized the DOJ in an effort to reject democracy. Over the past few months, Trump’s Justice Department filed a slew of federal lawsuits that aimed to limit who could vote; to control whether and how votes are counted; and to challenge election results. But so far, none of them have succeeded.
Last year, Trump demanded that nearly every state in the country hand over their complete, unredacted voter registration files and remove specific individuals upon request. The Justice Department sued 30 states and Washington, D.C., for refusing to do so. To date, at least 27 of those cases have been dismissed.
The Trump administration nonetheless cobbled together a list of tens of thousands of people who it contended were “likely” noncitizens, and went to court to demand their removal from the voter rolls. On October 13, after California had already mailed ballots to voters, the administration directed California to review its list within 48 hours, confirm the citizenship status of the listed individuals, and set aside the ballots of anyone whose citizenship they could not verify. When California did not comply, Trump’s Justice Department immediately sued, asking a federal district court to order the state to segregate and exclude more than 20,000 ballots.
Apparently unsatisfied with the pace of district court proceedings, Trump’s DOJ quickly filed an appeal, which construed the fact that the court had not issued a ruling yet as a “constructive denial.” On October 26, the Ninth Circuit dismissed the Justice Department’s appeal as premature. Two days later, the district court ruled against the Justice Department, too, rejecting the administration’s ploy as “unprecedented,” “unconstitutional,” and a “danger” to democracy.
Foiled again, Trump’s Justice Department recently tried a different gambit. Instead of trying to decide who votes and how the votes are counted, the DOJ filed a lawsuit to preemptively ignore the will of the voters. In Alaska, Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, is running for reelection against multiple candidates, including someone who is also named Dan Sullivan. The DOJ’s complaint contends that the inclusion of both Dan Sullivans on the ballot is “confusing to voters” and that any election results “tainted” by the challenger Sullivan must not be certified until an “investigation” determines if votes cast for the challenger were meant for the incumbent.
The Republican-led government of Alaska, the Democratic Senate candidate’s campaign, and nonpartisan organizations all filed motions to dismiss the DOJ’s complaint. And on November 1, Alaska’s federal district court granted all three motions, finding that the DOJ’s requested relief—investigating voters and segregating their ballots based on the candidates they selected—was “infeasible” and would “clearly violate Alaskans’ right to a secret ballot.”
Much like the villain in a Halloween movie, though, Trump’s DOJ never just stays down. Last week, The New York Times published an investigation into Alaska Democrats’ recruitment of the second Sullivan to run for senate. In response, the DOJ has already issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas and is flirting with the idea of criminal charges. Any such prosecution is unlikely to succeed—sometimes “conspiracies” are just funny, not criminal—but it creates another avenue for Trump to contest the legitimacy of the democratic process, and try to override any outcome he doesn’t like.
The Supreme Court has allowed and empowered Trump to try to overturn elections. But as this midterm season shows, the Court did not guarantee that Trump’s Justice Department would succeed. The elections also confirm, though, that Trump has many tools at his disposal to thwart the democratic process. And the Supreme Court gave him every incentive to keep trying his luck.

The emergency application came after a federal district judge and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit turned down the request.

U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer said in the emergency filing earlier in the day that the justices urgently needed to act. “Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back,” he said.

In the lower courts, they argued that the federal government has no standing to sue a state in federal court over how the state administers elections, that California’s own citizenship verification system already addresses noncitizen voting, and that segregating the ballots would violate federal election laws and risk disrupting the count.

The DOJ stated that California had failed to meet a deadline to complete a review of the suspected noncitizens, some of whom the department said had mailed in ballots.
President Donald Trump has said on multiple occasions that states are not doing enough to prevent noncitizens from voting.
The U.S. Constitution gives states primary authority to administer elections, but the federal government enjoys some oversight.
After the emergency application was filed, acting Deputy U.S. Attorney General Trent McCotter said California has “refused to work with the Federal Government to protect against noncitizen voting, which dilutes lawful votes,” so the DOJ filed an emergency application to require the state to segregate the mail ballots until the voters’ citizenship can be verified.

“If the United States believes different procedures are necessary for vote-by-mail ballots, we believe it should take that suggestion to Congress, not the courts,” the majority said.

The U.S. Department of Justice on Monday asked the U.S. Supreme Court to require California to set aside the ballots of suspected noncitizen voters in a last-ditch appeal by the Trump administration to exert control over the state’s vote counting.
The request came on the eve of Election Day and as more than 5 million mail ballots have already been cast in California, a state where voters are expected to elect dozens of Democrats to the U.S. House.
California’s election could be thrown into chaos if the Supreme Court grants the request. State and local election officials have previously warned that they have no easy way to quickly identify and set aside the ballots of individuals on the list.
In the Trump administration’s emergency application, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer noted that federal law prohibits voting by noncitizens, who still do sometimes vote “despite that prohibition,” he wrote.
“Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back,” Sauer added.
Logistically difficult
As a universal vote-by-mail state, every voter in California is sent a mail ballot. While millions of these ballots have already been returned, millions more may be dropped off on Tuesday or arrive by mail in the coming days.
Aman Bhullar, an assistant Los Angeles County registrar-recorder/county clerk, warned in a court declaration in October that the Trump administration’s request could wreak havoc on elections.
“The potential consequences of implementing DOJ’s demand are severe and range from halting all counting; halting in-person voters’ ability to cast votes; or otherwise interfering with the ability to accurately count votes,” Bhullar wrote.
Already a week ago, Shelby Wayment, staff attorney at the University of California, Los Angeles Safeguarding Democracy Project, questioned the feasibility of the DOJ’s demands. Ballots have already been mailed out and were being processed, she said.
“Just logistically, I don’t think it’s possible at this point,” Wayment said in a late October interview.
No widespread fraud
The Justice Department sued California in October, alleging that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security had identified 20,000 suspected noncitizen voters. California officials raised concerns about the veracity of the list, and declined to take action based on it.
An immigrant rights group, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, has raised serious concerns about the list after a judge forced the Trump administration to share a copy with the organization.
The group said in a court filing Saturday that an analysis by data experts found that 42% of the names weren’t found on California’s current voter file. At least 22 names on the list match names of U.S. citizens compiled by the organization, the analysis found.
“There is no widespread voter fraud. The federal government has no right to interfere in California’s elections,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said in a statement on Saturday.
11th hour challenge
The Justice Department has said the Department of Homeland Security compiled the list by checking a public copy of California’s voter file against federal records and information from the research service Lexis Nexis.
A district court judge and the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals have both ruled against the Trump administration in the case. State and local officials have argued the Justice Department exceeded its authority because states administer elections under the U.S. Constitution.
Even though the 9th Circuit issued a decision on Friday, the Justice Department didn’t ask the Supreme Court to intervene until midday Monday, less than 24 hours before Election Day.
The Justice Department has asked for an administrative stay that would require California to begin segregating ballots of voters on the list while the Trump administration prepares a full appeal. While it’s unknown how the Supreme Court will rule, in general the justices frown on federal courts ordering major last-minute changes to elections.
Because the case arises out of the 9th Circuit, Justice Elena Kagan, one of the court’s three liberals, will be the first to review the application.
Walter Olsen, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute’s Robert A. Levy Center for Constitutional Studies, in a statement predicted the Supreme Court will reject the request. He argued that the Justice Department is asking California officials to violate their own state laws.
“The Supreme Court should and I believe will reject the administration’s nervy last-minute attempts to meddle in California’s elections, as lower courts have rejected them,” Olsen said.

The dispute between the federal government and California election officials grew out of an effort to compare voter registration information with immigration and other records.
According to the Trump administration, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) used a publicly accessible version of the state's voter roll, supplemented by an investigative database. The government alleges that the process produced more than 20,000 people who appeared to be registered to vote in California, despite potentially being noncitizens. It then provided a list to California's Secretary of State Shirley Weber and the Los Angeles County Clerk, Dean Logan on October 13.

The California case fits into a wider Trump administration effort to place citizenship verification, voter-roll maintenance, and mail-in voting under greater federal control ahead of tomorrow's midterms.
Despite using the method himself, President Donald Trump has repeatedly cast doubt on the security of voting by mail, in part due to the time it takes some states to gather, count and verify these ballots.
At the same time, the president and others within his administration have raised concerns about noncitizen voting, claiming that potentially hundreds of thousands of registered voters are on rolls illegally, as they are not citizens.
The administration has sought voter registration data from nearly every state, including information states usually exclude from publicly available information, including birth dates and partial Social Security numbers. By late October, 30 lawsuits had been filed seeking voter data, with courts rejecting 27 of those cases.
There have been cases of noncitizens, including green card holders, voting in recent federal elections, with the DOJ and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) highlighting these cases in recent press releases. While some cases have been proven, the likely impact of these votes on the outcomes of elections is minimal, experts have said.
Another issue facing the federal government's efforts is that the administration of elections is left to the states, which all use differing systems. DHS has urged local officials to use its Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system to verify voter information, including their citizenship status, but not all states have adopted it and there have been concerns raised that not all databases are up-to-date, meaning immigration statuses being flagged may not be accurate.
Trump has urged Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require people registering to vote to produce documentary proof of citizenship, such as a birth certificate or naturalization certificate, after federal courts blocked those efforts through executive order.

The unusually fast decision underscored that the administration’s case, which was based on an uncertain methodology, was a reach that has been rejected by every court to consider it. The appeal also came to the high court on an exceedingly tight timeline — on the eve of the midterm election — with an unknown number of mail ballots in question likely already counted.
The court did not explain its reasoning and instead handed down only a one-sentence order. There were no noted dissents.
Tens of millions of voters have already cast early ballots nationwide.
“This office has been informed that the United States has identified more than 20,000 individuals who appear to be registered to vote in California based on publicly available information at the time that information was received, but who, in the United States’ view, are likely not U.S. citizens,” US Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the court earlier Monday.
In another sign that the Supreme Court didn’t take the appeal especially seriously, the justices did not ask to see a response brief from California or other parties before ruling – as is their usual practice in high-profile cases.
“After repeatedly losing in the lower courts, the highest court in the land firmly slapped down the Trump DOJ’s baseless attack on California’s electoral process — not even entertaining it,” Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom said in a statement.
The rapid decision marked another major loss for Trump on election cases at the high court. In September, the justices rejected the president’s controversial plan to change how mail ballots are sent to voters across the country, rebuffing a proposal that election officials warned would have had catastrophic consequences if allowed to take effect for this year’s midterms.
Sauer, the Trump administration’s top appellate attorney, urged the court to grant the “modest remedy” of setting aside any ballots cast by those individuals until the allegations could be resolved.
DOJ had argued the federal government had a constitutional interest in ensuring that only citizens vote. It also claims that California’s failure to investigate the registered voters the administration has flagged is frustrating enforcement of the federal criminal law banning noncitizen voting.
California and voting rights groups countered that the federal government’s past claims of noncitizen voters have not withstood scrutiny, that the current claims are based on fuzzy evidence that risks disenfranchising citizens and that the Trump administration doesn’t have authority to tell state officials how to handle the issue. Those are arguments that found purchase in lower federal courts that ruled against Trump.
“Every court to hear this case has now rejected the DOJ’s attempt to cast a cloud of suspicion over eligible voters’ ballots on the eve of an election,” said Uzoma Nkwonta, with the Elias Law Group, which represented groups opposed to the Trump administration suit.
On Friday, the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals barred the administration from intervening in California’s mail-in ballot counting, concluding that the federal government has no power to dictate to states how to run elections.
“If the United States believes different procedures are necessary for vote-by-mail ballots, we believe it should take that suggestion to Congress, not the courts,” the appeals court wrote in a 2-1 decision that was issued by US Circuit Judges Mark Bennett, a Trump nominee, and Gabriel Sanchez, who was named to the bench by former President Joe Biden.
“The district court found that the risks that noncitizens are voting are, at best, uncertain, and also tempered by California’s established voter-eligibility procedures,” the 9th Circuit wrote Friday. “In contrast, there is a material risk that granting the United States its requested relief would result in disenfranchisement.”
In his dissent, US Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay noted that the Trump administration was asking only to halt the mixing of ballots cast by citizens and alleged noncitizens. Once those ballots are processed, all sides agree, it would be impossible to separate them.
“Throughout history, federal courts have acted to protect the voting and civil rights of our citizens by enjoining state action that violates the law,” wrote Bumatay, a Trump nominee. “And common sense also tells us that the federal government shouldn’t have to sit on its hands while a state allows the violation of federal law, especially when the integrity of federal elections is at stake.”
The appeals court also raised an issue that could be decisive for the Supreme Court. Under a legal theory known as the “Purcell principle,” the justices have long warned against federal courts weighing in at the last minute to change the rules of an election.
Trump has had a mixed record with emergency election appeals at the Supreme Court. Most notably, the justices in September rejected the president’s attempt to give the US Postal Service extraordinary power to withhold certain mail ballots. But the court sided with the Department of Homeland Security days later, allowing it to continue providing controversial citizenship data to state election officials.
“The federal government continues to press the same arguments, despite repeatedly coming up short,” said Jon Miller, chief program officer at Public Rights Project, which is part of the legal team fighting the Justice Department. “This case has bounced between the appellate and district courts – and every time, the courts have found the Justice Department wasn’t entitled to the relief it was seeking.”

sources.news_title: Trump’s DOJ Turns to Supreme Court in California Ballot Clash
Trump asks Supreme Court to segregate California ballots
sources.text:
(The Center Square) - The Trump administration on Monday asked justices on the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene as it seeks to segregate mail-in ballots in California over fears of noncitizens voting.
The U.S. Department of Justice asked justices on the high court to temporarily block an order from a lower court judge preventing nearly 20,000 individual ballots from being segregated. The appeal to the high court comes one day before the 2026 midterm elections, where stakes are high as legal battles surmount across the country.
Solicitor General John Sauer said the measure was a necessary step to ensure the integrity of federal elections across California. The state sends mail-in ballots to every registered voter leading up to an election.
"Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," Sauer wrote in a filing. "The only way to preserve the district court's ability to grant relief to the United States after a full merits proceeding, therefore, is to segregate the challenged ballots now."
On Oct. 13, the Justice Department warned the California Secretary of State's office about 20,000 "highly likely" noncitizen voters. Election officials in California said the effort would create confusion for voters and sow distrust in the system.
Kiersten Pels, a spokesperson with the Justice Department, told The Center Square 28 people on that list were charged with federal crimes, including lying about their citizenship to vote.
“What undermines confidence is noncitizens voting,” said Pels. “Eligible citizens are not affected. We asked counties to set aside these ballots, not cancel them, until citizenship is confirmed.”
California Attorney General Rob Bonta has repeatedly dismissed claims of noncitizen voting in the state's elections.
"Their is no widespread voter fraud. The federal government has no right to interfere in California's elections," Bonta wrote on social media Saturday.
On Oct. 28, U.S. District Judge David Carter ruled against the Trump administration's request to segregate ballots.
"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," Carter, a Clinton appointee, wrote in his ruling. "In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too."
Justices on the high court could act on the Trump administration's request at any time, but there is no deadline to respond.

sources.news_title: Day before election, Trump’s DOJ asks US Supreme Court to rule in California voting case - Now Georgia
sources.text:
The U.S. Department of Justice on Monday asked the U.S. Supreme Court to require California to set aside the ballots of suspected noncitizen voters in a last-ditch appeal by the Trump administration to exert control over the state’s vote counting.
The request came on the eve of Election Day and as more than 5 million mail ballots have already been cast in California, a state where voters are expected to elect dozens of Democrats to the U.S. House.
California’s election could be thrown into chaos if the Supreme Court grants the request. State and local election officials have previously warned that they have no easy way to quickly identify and set aside the ballots of individuals on the list.
In the Trump administration’s emergency application, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer noted that federal law prohibits voting by noncitizens, who still do sometimes vote “despite that prohibition,” he wrote.
“Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back,” Sauer added.
Logistically difficult
As a universal vote-by-mail state, every voter in California is sent a mail ballot. While millions of these ballots have already been returned, millions more may be dropped off on Tuesday or arrive by mail in the coming days.
Aman Bhullar, an assistant Los Angeles County registrar-recorder/county clerk, warned in a court declaration in October that the Trump administration’s request could wreak havoc on elections.
“The potential consequences of implementing DOJ’s demand are severe and range from halting all counting; halting in-person voters’ ability to cast votes; or otherwise interfering with the ability to accurately count votes,” Bhullar wrote.
Already a week ago, Shelby Wayment, staff attorney at the University of California, Los Angeles Safeguarding Democracy Project, questioned the feasibility of the DOJ’s demands. Ballots have already been mailed out and were being processed, she said.
“Just logistically, I don’t think it’s possible at this point,” Wayment said in a late October interview.
No widespread fraud
The Justice Department sued California in October, alleging that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security had identified 20,000 suspected noncitizen voters. California officials raised concerns about the veracity of the list, and declined to take action based on it.
An immigrant rights group, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, has raised serious concerns about the list after a judge forced the Trump administration to share a copy with the organization.
The group said in a court filing Saturday that an analysis by data experts found that 42% of the names weren’t found on California’s current voter file. At least 22 names on the list match names of U.S. citizens compiled by the organization, the analysis found.
“There is no widespread voter fraud. The federal government has no right to interfere in California’s elections,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said in a statement on Saturday.
11th hour challenge
The Justice Department has said the Department of Homeland Security compiled the list by checking a public copy of California’s voter file against federal records and information from the research service Lexis Nexis.
A district court judge and the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals have both ruled against the Trump administration in the case. State and local officials have argued the Justice Department exceeded its authority because states administer elections under the U.S. Constitution.
Even though the 9th Circuit issued a decision on Friday, the Justice Department didn’t ask the Supreme Court to intervene until midday Monday, less than 24 hours before Election Day.
The Justice Department has asked for an administrative stay that would require California to begin segregating ballots of voters on the list while the Trump administration prepares a full appeal. While it’s unknown how the Supreme Court will rule, in general the justices frown on federal courts ordering major last-minute changes to elections.
Because the case arises out of the 9th Circuit, Justice Elena Kagan, one of the court’s three liberals, will be the first to review the application.
Walter Olsen, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute’s Robert A. Levy Center for Constitutional Studies, in a statement predicted the Supreme Court will reject the request. He argued that the Justice Department is asking California officials to violate their own state laws.
“The Supreme Court should and I believe will reject the administration’s nervy last-minute attempts to meddle in California’s elections, as lower courts have rejected them,” Olsen said.
